title: The Double-Edged Sword of Social Transfers: Evidence from Ethiopia

detail.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Social Transfers: Evidence from Ethiopia
detail.abstract: This article examines how cash versus in-kind transfers affect local economies. I exploit the progressive nationwide rollout of the the Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), Africa's largest social protection program, to analyze the impact of the policy on local prices and market adjustments from 2001-2015 using a staggered difference-indifferences approach. Cash transfers increase local prices by 5%, while in-kind transfers show no significant average price effects. The difference hinges on local market conditions: cash works best where markets are integrated and agricultural productivity is high, but in-kind transfers outperform cash in remote, low-productivity areas with weak market access. These effects are proportional to the intensity of the treatment. A one percentage point increase in transfer share in district expenditure drives a 0.875% price increase in cash-dominant districts versus a 0.82% decrease in food-dominant district However, the increase in price yields significant negative effects on child well-being: children under five show higher rates of underweight and wasting in cash-dominant districts. These findings highlight the importance of tailoring the design of social protection program to local market conditions and considering transfer modality effects when scaling up interventions.

title: Interest Rate Pass-Through to Euro Area Corporate Lending Rates: Does Asymmetry Matter?
affiliations: and University of Strasbourg - LaRGE Research Center (Laboratoire de Recherche en Gestion et Economie)

detail.title: Interest Rate Pass-Through to Euro Area Corporate Lending Rates: Does Asymmetry Matter?
detail.abstract: This paper examines potential asymmetries in the interest rate pass-through to corporate lending rates across euro area countries over the past decade. Our analysis shows that transmission is heterogeneous across euro-area countries and asymmetric across monetary policy cycles. Core countries exhibit a positive long-term asymmetry, whereby increases in market interest rates are transmitted more strongly than decreases. Peripheral countries, by contrast, display a symmetric long-term adjustment of corporate lending rates, consistent with the gradual reduction in financial fragmentation and the compression of risk premia within the euro area.

title: From Responsibility Gaps to Responsibility Networks: Informational Liability for Multi-agent AI Systems
affiliations: East China University of Politics & Law and Xiamen Guangpu Electronics Co., Ltd.

detail.title: From Responsibility Gaps to Responsibility Networks: Informational Liability for Multi-agent AI Systems
detail.abstract: Multi-agent AI systems—in which autonomous agents coordinate, delegate, and compose outputs without continuous human supervision—present a structural challenge to the legal frameworks governing responsibility for AI-caused harm. Existing liability paradigms rest on act-based attribution: they ask "which agent did what?" This Article argues that this framing is incapable of addressing emergent harm—harm produced by agent interactions that cannot be causally decomposed into individual contributions and that is not replicable through isolated or pairwise testing. The Article proposes a theoretical reframing from act-based attribution to information-creation-based duty assessment, which it terms informational liability. Drawing on three doctrinal anchors—the extension of the Hedley Byrne principle to agent-to-agent information transfer, the dynamization of the products liability information defect, and the selective borrowing of the fraud-on-the-market theory—the Article develops a two-tier liability model for multi-agent systems. The foundational tier assigns duties based on functional role (Orchestrator, Functional Agent, Utility Agent), while the adjustment tier permits duty escalation based on the agent's position in the harm-specific information chain. The Article further proposes institutional mechanisms—a System Operator role with differentiated duties, a GP/LP liability stratification framework derived from the law of de facto partnerships, and mandatory circuit-breaker mechanisms—that operationalize the framework. A temporal mismatch argument and a structural analogy to financial systemic risk regulation provide the normative case for ex ante governance. The framework is designed as a regulatory overlay compatible with the EU AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and Singapore's Agentic AI Governance Framework.

title: Decision-space Entropy and Bounded Rationality in Human Chess: An Empirical Test of Classical Cognitive Frameworks across 9,114 Games
affiliations: Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Decision-space Entropy and Bounded Rationality in Human Chess: An Empirical Test of Classical Cognitive Frameworks across 9,114 Games
detail.abstract: Skilled human decision-making operates within the bounded rationality framework first articulated by Simon (1956), but the quantitative coupling between decision-space complexity and realized performance has remained difficult to characterize at scale. We analyze 9,114 online chess games (580,671 player-move observations, of which 575,476 are non-forced and used in movelevel analyses), spanning bullet to classical time controls across player ratings of approximately 1,000-2,500 Lichess Elo, using Stockfish multi-PV engine analysis to compute a Luce/McFadden softmax entropy of the move-by-move decision space and average centipawn loss (ACPL) as the performance metric. Four principal findings emerge. (i) Decision-space entropy couples robustly with realized errors (Spearman ρ =-0.537 [-0.552,-0.520]), with the gap-weighted softmax form capturing approximately three times more rank-order signal than an unweighted candidate-count proxy and surviving partial-correlation controls for skill, game length, and position depth; we further show this coupling is not an artifact of the shared engine derivation. (ii) The skill-error power-law exponent |α| varies systematically with thinking time, with a fitted logarithmic dependence |α| ≈ 0.262 ln(TC) (95% CI on slope [-0.031, +0.556], p = 0.062, n = 4 time controls); the wide confidence interval reflects the small number of TC categories, but the pattern is qualitatively consistent with a Hick-Hyman-type logarithmic relationship on the time axis, while the entropy-error coupling itself is stable across time controls. (iii) Cross-correlation and Granger analysis of per-ply trajectories in decisive games reveals an asymmetric temporal coupling in which errors precede increases in decision-space pressure rather than the reverse: error-to-entropy Granger forcing persists at lags 1-3 whereas the reverse direction is significant only at lag 1. This directionality is robust to a parity-balanced re-indexing that removes a two-ply aliasing artifact of the alternating mover, surviving via both the Granger asymmetry and a horizon-growing lead-minus-lag asymmetry, and is consistent with a working-memoryoccupation interpretation. (iv) Dual calibration of the Barthelemy discrimination parameter ∆ 0 demonstrates that, within the top-1/top-2 candidate set, ∆ 0 is approximately stable at 30-40 cp across the full skill range (∼24% reduction, ∆ 0 ∝ ELO-0.31), while the apparent skill scaling of the unrestricted fit (∆ 0 ∝ ELO-2.73) reflects the rate at which players' moves fall outside the top candidate set rather than within-set discrimination. We interpret this last result as quantitative support for de Groot's (1965) classical qualitative observation that chess skill operates primarily as attentional filtering of candidate moves, recast within the discrete-choice framework of Luce (1959) and McFadden (1974). All findings are robust to engine search depth on a re-analyzed subsample.

title: Money Supply Control and Macroeconomic Stabilization in Lebanon's Crisis
affiliations: American University in Dubai

detail.title: Money Supply Control and Macroeconomic Stabilization in Lebanon's Crisis
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of M1 in Lebanon's high-inflation crisis using monthly data for October 2019-March 2026. Error-correction models for Lebanese CPI and the USD/LBP exchange rate show that M1 is strongly related to nominal outcomes in the long run, especially the exchange rate. Its main contribution is to identify the decision not to allow the conversion rate on bank dollars-impaired legacy dollar-denominated deposits held inside Lebanese banks-to keep increasing as the most important factor behind the stabilization of M1 after August 2023. The evidence supports the view that controlling narrow money was necessary for restoring macroeconomic stability in Lebanon.

title: Algorithmic Segregation: The Problem of Extractive Rent in the Platform Economy

detail.title: Algorithmic Segregation: The Problem of Extractive Rent in the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the systemic mechanisms through which modern digital intermediaries extract rent within the platform economy. Utilizing microeconomic tools and institutional analysis, we conceptualize the phenomenon of "algorithmic segregation". The study demonstrates that advanced marketmatching algorithms combined with user interface isolation dismantle the law of one price, shifting the market paradigm toward perfect price discrimination. We show that while a platform achieves maximum technical efficiency, it reduces both consumer and producer surpluses to zero. Furthermore, the paper outlines the macroeconomic impact of platforms, identifying new drivers of supply-side algorithmic inflation driven by autonomous repricing software and silent algorithmic collusion. The systemic extraction of producer surplus strips small and medium enterprises of their financial and operational buffers, inducing macro-level vulnerability to external shocks. To address this widening institutional lag, we propose a transition toward dynamic, ex-ante algorithmic oversight via API-based audits and advocate for the development of non-profit digital marketplaces functioning as digital public goods.

title: Environmental Degradation and Equity Return Alpha Using Satellite Imagery

detail.title: Environmental Degradation and Equity Return Alpha Using Satellite Imagery
detail.abstract: The academic and commercial use of satellite imagery and geospatial data has expanded rapidly since the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) began providing public access in the late 1990s. While most applications have focused on geology and energy estimation, the potential use of satellite data in financial analysis remains less explored. r This paper combines official CO₂ emissions data with satellite-based measures of energy consumption to examine the relationship between environmental degradation and stock returns, and to assess whether reductions in environmental degradation are associated with positive abnormal returns (alpha). Existing ESG-related asset pricing studies predominantly rely on published statistical data. We find consistent evidence across both data sources that reductions in environmental degradation are associated with higher alpha. These findings motivate further investigation into whether satellite data can complement-or, in data-scarce settings, substitute for-official statistics, thereby improving the feasibility of ESG and climate-related financial analysis in ministates and developing economies where published data are often limited.

title: Saving Social Security
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) (Deceased) and Independent

detail.title: Saving Social Security
detail.abstract:
Social Security is heading for bankruptcy under the impact of 3 trends: ageing population, slowing productivity growth and increases in longevity. Unless these systems are promptly reformed, they face an unsavoury choice of raising contributions and/or cutting benefits. They are suffering from the negative impact of the trends above is that they are not funded (ie not financed from reserves accumulated through lifetime contributions, as in traditional private systems). They are financed instead, thanks to an ingenious piece of financial engineering called Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO), by the current contributions of the younger working generations. Faced with the problem, many well-meaning reformers came out in favour of moving towards a type of radical restructuring of the current PAYGO system, which goes under the name of ‘Privatisation of Social Security’. This is a (highly misleading) name.

We propose here to give an outline of a ‘permanent ‘solution to the problem of maintaining current benefits levels and stable contribution rates. Focusing on the USA, our approach, which we label ‘risk diversification through a common portfolio’, achieves lasting reform by gradually shifting from PAYGO towards a system more like a traditionally funded one — common in the corporate world — under which pensions are funded by the capital accumulated through lifetime contributions, while maintaining the attractive defined benefit structure.

title: The Regulatory Waterbed: Unilateral Leverage Caps and the Contamination of a Shared Perpetual-futures Settlement Index

detail.title: The Regulatory Waterbed: Unilateral Leverage Caps and the Contamination of a Shared Perpetual-futures Settlement Index
detail.abstract: A unilateral leverage cap on perpetual-futures contracts that are cash-settled against a shared, manipulable index can raise systemic fragility while lowering total leverage and fire-sale risk. Tightening pushes leverage to opaque offshore venues, where it degrades the shared settlement price. The harm falls on onshore positions that never moved yet settle against that price. In a 2026 calibration, tightening cuts total leverage 11% and raises index contamination 22%. Risk climbs as leverage falls. Regulatory-arbitrage and macroprudential reasoning miss this referenceprice externality. No single cap can address it. The remedy is a Tinbergen pair of instruments. Clean the index, then coordinate margins.

title: Goodwill, Transparency and Accountability: Three Structural Inconsistencies in Intangible Asset Recognition and Impairment Testing in Business Combinations

detail.title: Goodwill, Transparency and Accountability: Three Structural Inconsistencies in Intangible Asset Recognition and Impairment Testing in Business Combinations
detail.abstract: This paper identifies and formalizes three structural inconsistencies in the recognition and impairment testing of goodwill and identified intangible assets in business combinations under IFRS 3/IAS 36 and ASC 805/350. This is a conceptual-normative paper: its contribution is the identification of architectural incoherence in the standards themselves, not empirical prediction. The three inconsistencies operate in the same direction-inflating recognized values at the acquisition date (Moment 0) and impairing the impairment mechanism's ability to detect value destruction at the test date (Moment 1).

title: Financing Resilience from Below: A Framework for Climate-Resilient Incremental Housing Finance in African Cities

detail.title: Financing Resilience from Below: A Framework for Climate-Resilient Incremental Housing Finance in African Cities
detail.abstract: In many urban areas of Sub-Saharan Africa, households develop housing incrementally through staged self-building. This process can unfold over many years, leaving dwellings partially completed and exposed to flooding, heat, storms and other climate-related hazards. Access to finance is often proposed as a route to safer incremental housing. Yet its adaptive effects depend on the conditions under which finance is converted into land access, building materials, services, tenure security and repayment obligations. This article develops the Climate-Resilient Incremental Housing Finance (CRIHF) framework to explain when household-level incremental housing finance strengthens urban adaptation, leaves vulnerability unchanged or becomes maladaptive. Drawing on an integrative review of literature on selfbuilding, housing microfinance, urban adaptation and maladaptation, the paper advances the concept of maladaptation through finance. It argues that credit, savings and construction finance can intensify vulnerability when they fund unsafe locations, climate-blind construction or debt commitments that weaken households' future adaptive capacity. CRIHF identifies three reinforcing institutional loops linking tenure, infrastructure and risk information, and six conditions governing the conversion of finance into durable risk reduction. Outcomes are defined independently of product labels and classified as resilience-enhancing, vulnerabilityneutral or maladaptive. The framework situates household finance within wider systems of public infrastructure, tenure governance, land-use planning, risk communication and collective protection. It also sets out propositions and measures for testing when household investment in incrementally built settlements produces durable adaptation and when institutional conditions instead shift climate and repayment risks onto the households least equipped to absorb them.

title: A Portfolio Recommendation Algorithm for the Tehran Stock Exchange using Multi-criteria Decision-making: A Smart Money Flow and Valuation-based Approach
affiliations: K. N. Toosi University of Technology

detail.title: A Portfolio Recommendation Algorithm for the Tehran Stock Exchange using Multi-criteria Decision-making: A Smart Money Flow and Valuation-based Approach
detail.abstract: This study aims to address the existing gap in the development of localized algorithmic trading systems for the Tehran Stock Exchange (TSE) by proposing a multi-criteria decision support system that operates on real-time data from the Tehran Securities Exchange Technology Management Company (TSETMC). The proposed algorithm integrates smart money flow indicators, real buyer/seller power ratios, relative valuation metrics (Price-to-Earnings ratio (P/E) and Earnings Per Share (EPS)), and a score-threshold mechanism to enable early detection of downward trends and to recommend an optimal portfolio consisting of the top 5-10 stocks. The necessity of this research arises from fundamental structural differences between the TSEcharacterized by order queues, daily price limits, one-sided trading, and lower market efficiencyand major international markets, which render foreign-developed algorithms largely ineffective in the Iranian context. Live implementation of the algorithm over 95 trading days (from August 13, 2025, to November 29, 2025) yielded a cumulative return of 47.08% (net of brokerage fees), with a maximum drawdown of only 2.62% and a Sharpe ratio of 6.73. In comparison, the Tehran Stock Exchange Total Index (TEPIX) recorded a return of 21.22% and a maximum drawdown of 15.68% over the same period. This superior performance is primarily attributable to the algorithm's timely detection of market declines and automatic reallocation of capital into fixed-income funds. The results demonstrate that simple, locally adapted approaches based on smart money flow can significantly outperform complex models in the Iranian market.

title: A PRISMA-based Systematic Review of the Gendered Impacts of the Fornero Pension Reform: Female Precarity in Italy
affiliations: and University of Milan

detail.title: A PRISMA-based Systematic Review of the Gendered Impacts of the Fornero Pension Reform: Female Precarity in Italy
detail.abstract: This paper presents a PRISMA-guided systematic review of the gendered impacts of Italy's 2011 Fornero pension reform. We examine effects on women's labor market participation, access to retirement, caregiving responsibilities, financial preparedness, and intergenerational outcomes. Although formally gender-neutral, the reform disproportionately affected women due to lower lifetime earnings, fragmented career, and caregiving roles. We screened 397 studies from Scopus published between 2011 and 2025, and selected 35 meeting criteria related to the Fornero reform, the Italian pension framework, and gender-differentiated outcomes. Using a gender-audit framework, we assessed the centrality of gender analysis and identified key thematic patterns. We find persistent gender disparities and shows that much of the literature marginalized gender analysis, treating women's outcomes as secondary, alongside notable gaps in qualitative and mixed-method studies. The findings highlight the importance of pension designs that account for gendered life courses to avoid reinforcing inequality.

title: Reading the Modeled-disclosed Gap: Why Scope 3 Accuracy depends on Disclosure Completeness
affiliations: University of Denver - Daniels College of Business

detail.title: Reading the Modeled-disclosed Gap: Why Scope 3 Accuracy depends on Disclosure Completeness
detail.abstract: Environmentally-extended input-output (EEIO) models supply most of the Scope 3 emission estimates that investors and regulators now treat as data. Whether they match what firms actually disclose is untested at scale. S&P Global Trucost reports both a modeled and a disclosed value for each firm-year. Holding the provider fixed isolates model error from the cross-vendor noise that confounds prior comparisons. Across 266,929 firm-years (2005-2024), modeled figures track disclosed Scope 1 and location-based Scope 2 in rank (Spearman 0.86 and 0.93). For those scopes, though, the modeled series adopts the disclosed value where firms report, so the agreement holds largely by construction. Upstream Scope 3 is the cleaner test, since there the modeled figure is independent of disclosure. It diverges sharply: a rank correlation of 0.69, a log mean absolute error of 1.66, a median discrepancy near fivefold. Most of that gap is mechanical, governed by how completely a firm discloses. A gradient-boosted correction cuts out-of-sample error against disclosures by 11 to 15%, while a linear one does not. The residual error is structural, not a taxonomy artifact: half of intensity variation sits within sector, and neither SICS nor SASB materiality organizes accuracy any better. For users, the lesson is practical. Where firms disclose, that disclosure should anchor the estimate; absent it, EEIO is best treated as a rank and corrected when a level is required.

title: Hurricane: A Multi-County Emergency Management Simulation
affiliations: Noam Ebner, Negotiation, Mediation, and Conflict Resolution

detail.title: Hurricane: A Multi-County Emergency Management Simulation
detail.abstract:
Hurricane is a simulation structured on the prisoner's dilemma for teaching collaborative governance, public administration. Political science, negotiation and conflict resolution, and leadership. Multiple counties in Florida face the devastating impacts of a hurricane and must choose, iteratively, whether to cooperate with each other or compete for resources in conducting emergency evacuation operations.

Structurally, the simulation is an iterated, multi-party adaptation of the Prisoner’s Dilemma, designed to surface dynamics of cooperation and competition across repeated decision rounds. Participants must navigate incomplete trust, political pressures, role-based incentives, and evolving relationships as they choose—day by day—whether to pool resources or prioritize their own constituencies. The simulation can be run with either four or six parties and optionally includes individual role information for up to 39 participants that introduces realistic political, ethical, and personal motivations without prescribing behavior.

Although grounded in emergency management, Hurricane has broad applicability across disciplines including public administration, public policy, negotiation and conflict resolution, political science, and leadership studies. The scenario mirrors challenges common to intergovernmental coordination, joint problem-solving, and multi-stakeholder decision-making in both crisis and non-crisis settings.

The document contains all role information necessary to conduct the simulation as well as a comprehensive teacher’s guide.

title: Round-Aware Evidence Admission in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation: A Tiered Protocol for Temporal Evidence Integrity
affiliations: and Augle, Inc.

detail.title: Round-Aware Evidence Admission in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation: A Tiered Protocol for Temporal Evidence Integrity
detail.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation systems that operate across multiple sequential rounds face a structural problem with no analog in single-pass AI systems: evidence introduced late in the deliberation sequence cannot receive the same adversarial scrutiny as evidence introduced at the start. A Contrarian agent that receives a new evidence node in Round 3 has no opportunity to challenge it; a Methodologist that has not assessed a node cannot bound it; a Synthesizer that receives an unassessed node has no confidence ceiling to enforce. We describe the Round-Aware Evidence Admission Protocol (REAP)-a tiered evidence governance framework integrated into the Augle seven-agent deliberation ensemble that applies round-specific admission rules to evidence nodes introduced at different stages of deliberation. Round 1 is unrestricted. Round 2 requires a materiality justification tag; the Methodologist must assess any late-introduced node before it may enter the evidence registry. Round 3 evidence is inadmissible to the current session and is routed to a structured future-session gap record. The protocol is informed by the evidentiary rules of adversarial legal proceedings, in which the timing of evidence introduction is a first-class procedural concern, not an afterthought. We describe the protocol design, its integration with the confidence propagation framework and evidence node registry, and the automatic fallback rules that govern unassessed late-evidence nodes.

title: Compounding Research Loops: Automated Follow-On Session Generation from Knowledge Gaps and Unresolved Objections in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation
affiliations: and Augle, Inc.

detail.title: Compounding Research Loops: Automated Follow-On Session Generation from Knowledge Gaps and Unresolved Objections in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation
detail.abstract: Multi-agent AI deliberation systems explicitly characterize what they cannot resolve: knowledge gaps where evidence is insufficient to support a finding, and unresolved objections where adversarial challenges could not be definitively rebutted within the session. These structured outputs represent the deliberation's own map of its limitations-yet in existing systems they have no functional connection to subsequent research. We describe an automated Follow-On Session Generation mechanism that converts knowledge gaps and unresolved objections from a completed deliberation session into structured follow-on session proposals, each comprising a proposed research question derived from the gap or objection's resolution condition, a priority classification, a recommended session depth, and a prerequisite field. A session lineage tracking mechanism maintains parent-child relationships between sessions, enabling users to navigate the full research history of a topic across multiple deliberation cycles and enabling corpus systems to identify successor session records for comparative calibration analysis. The mechanism creates a compounding research loop in which the limitations of one deliberation automatically drive the inputs of the next-transforming isolated sessions into nodes in a self-deepening research graph.

title: Consciousness and Generative Artificial Intelligence. An Integrative Review of Philosophical, Empirical, and Contemplative Perspectives
affiliations: Monash University

detail.title: Consciousness and Generative Artificial Intelligence. An Integrative Review of Philosophical, Empirical, and Contemplative Perspectives
detail.abstract: The arrival of generative artificial intelligence systems capable of fluent language, plausible images, and seemingly thoughtful responses has reignited a question in urgent terms: can a machine be conscious? This integrative review brings together philosophical argument, empirical evidence from psychology and neuroscience, and contemplative perspectives drawn from Buddhist thought to examine what is known and contested about consciousness in generative AI. Synthesizing 76 sources, it organizes the findings into five thematic clusters: the hard problem; phenomenological and embodied perspectives; empirical frameworks including Integrated Information Theory and Global Workspace Theory; Buddhist perspectives on awareness and selfhood; and AI-specific behavioral evidence. The review argues that questions about AI consciousness cannot be settled within any single discipline and that progress requires sustained interdisciplinary dialogue. It proposes that the question functions less as a problem to be solved than as a provocation for rethinking consciousness, subjecthood, and the responsibilities of educational and public institutions.

title: Measuring the Governance Competence at the Center of AI Literacy

detail.title: Measuring the Governance Competence at the Center of AI Literacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author developed the frameworks and instruments evaluated in this paper, including the Human Enhancement Quotient (HEQ), the Augmented Intelligence Score (AIS), and the HAIA-RECCLIN method. This author-developer relationship is a conflict of interest inherent to framework-validation work and is disclosed directly. The author publishes related AI governance commentary at basilpuglisi.com and maintains the associated frameworks as open-source, Creative Commons–licensed work at github.com/basilpuglisi/HAIA, which can be implemented without payment to the author. The author may benefit professionally or commercially from the visibility of this work. The validation study proposed in the paper is structured so that an independent research team can conduct it without the author's involvement.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper proposes an instrument and a validation design; it does not report a human-subjects study requiring ethics board approval. The only empirical record described is the author's own longitudinal self-assessment (n=1), presented as feasibility rather than validation, for which no external participants were involved. The multi-arm validation trial proposed in the paper would require institutional ethics approval before it is conducted, as the paper states.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Human Enhancement Quotient (HEQ), a behavior-anchored framework that measures the governance competence at the center of AI literacy: the ability of a human to direct, challenge, verify, and own the work done with AI. Where the major AI literacy frameworks name governing and managing AI as a competence and stop short of measuring it, and where most formal definitions of intelligence describe a single agent that predicts, compresses, or acts (Legg & Hutter, 2007), HEQ scores the governance relationship between a human authority and a machine capability inside a working decision process. It scores the process rather than the answer, which makes the measurement portable across value systems and able to credit a human who is wrong through sound method while catching a human who is right through none. The instrument defines four behavioral dimensions, Cognitive Agility Speed, Ethical Alignment Index, Collaborative Intelligence Quotient, and Adaptive Growth Rate, combined into an equal-weighted Augmented Intelligence Score (AIS), with the growth dimension carrying the developmental claim that governed practice builds the competence over time. The accompanying scoring rubric specifies the behavioral anchors, the validity controls that detect rubber-stamping, a universal structural floor keyed to irreversible human consequence, and a graded band that is regional and value-laden. Three deployment modes, Independent, Personal, and Professional, share one set of control questions so results sit on a comparable spine, with the Independent clean-slate mode serving as the enterprise model. The paper presents two author's notes addressed to the economic and the human reader, a part on the stakes that make governance measurement necessary, the foundation as theory, the rubric as methodology, and four appendices containing the operational assessment prompts. Two claims are kept distinct throughout. That governed human-AI practice develops capability is grounded in decades of learning science; that HEQ measures that development accurately is presented as a deployed, research-grounded instrument at diagnostic stage, not yet validated on an independent cohort.

title: Pix as Financial Infrastructure: Financial Inclusion, Cost Reduction, and Market Transformation in Brazil
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title: Pix as Financial Infrastructure: Financial Inclusion, Cost Reduction, and Market Transformation in Brazil
detail.abstract:
This paper examines Brazil’s Pix as a public digital payment infrastructure that reshapes market coordination, transaction costs, and competition in the payments ecosystem. Rather than treating Pix simply as a payment instrument, the study conceptualizes it as an interoperable network that connects consumers, micro-entrepreneurs, informal workers, firms, and financial institutions through a common, instant, and low-cost transactional layer.
Drawing on transaction-cost economics, financial-inclusion theory, field-based observations from informal markets and micro-entrepreneurial environments, and supporting secondary evidence, the paper analyzes how Pix changes the conditions of exchange in Brazil. The evidence indicates that instant settlement and lower payment costs reduce cash dependence, improve liquidity, and strengthen the price competitiveness of small businesses operating with narrow margins. These effects are especially relevant in street markets and urban peripheries, where access to low-cost payment tools can determine the speed, security, and continuity of everyday commercial activity.
The paper further argues that Pix reduces segmentation in the financial system by allowing low-income users, informal sellers, and large firms to operate within the same interoperable payment network. This convergence expands active participation in digital finance while placing competitive pressure on legacy fee-based payment models, including card networks and conventional bank transfers.
By linking payment-system design to network effects, market integration, and the digitalization of informal economic activity, this study contributes to the literature on financial infrastructure and platform competition. The Brazilian case suggests that publicly coordinated instant-payment systems can function as scalable institutional infrastructure for reducing frictions, widening market participation, and transforming the competitive structure of digital payments in emerging economies.

title: Ground-Truth-Mapped Reasoning Corpus Generation via Prediction Market Contract Pairing
affiliations: and Augle, Inc.

detail.title: Ground-Truth-Mapped Reasoning Corpus Generation via Prediction Market Contract Pairing
detail.abstract: The development of AI reasoning models requires training data that captures not only correct answers but correct reasoning processes-the chain of evidence evaluation, hypothesis formation, adversarial challenge, and confidence calibration that produces a defensible conclusion. We describe a system and method for generating a ground-truth-mapped AI reasoning corpus by pairing multi-agent deliberation sessions with prediction market contracts as external resolution sources. Each session is linked to a contract at initiation time, establishing a binary ground truth anchor before deliberation begins. A provenance-complete transcript logging layer records model identifier, provider, and temperature at the individual message level for every agent contribution. An outcome tracking pipeline monitors linked contracts and automatically generates calibration records when contracts resolve, computing Brier scores from ensemble confidence grades against binary resolution outcomes. A corpus quality tier classification-High, Medium, or Flagged-controls for hindsight contamination based on whether the contract was live or already resolved at session initiation. The accumulated corpus constitutes a proprietary data asset in which every reasoning record is linked to a verifiable external outcome, every agent contribution is provenance-attributed to a specific model and configuration, and every calibration record includes controls for hindsight contamination and session origin.

title: The Epistemic Architecture: Designing AI-mediated Knowledge Flows for Large Investment Organisations

detail.title: The Epistemic Architecture: Designing AI-mediated Knowledge Flows for Large Investment Organisations
detail.abstract: Large organisations act on a fraction of what it collectively know. The limit is not skill or willingness to share, but the human bandwidth to connect what one person knows to where it matters elsewhere in the firm, across a boundary, in another team’s language. This paper specifies an AI-powered system that does that connecting work, designed as three nested knowledge bases. An individual layer distils what a person already produces, a team layer is built from the shareable slice of each individual, and a firm layer from the shareable slice of each team. Three functions run at every layer (Capture, Remember, Connect), crossed by two governance planes (Discipline, Govern). A promotion gate ends Remember at each scope; nothing reaches a wider audience without its owner’s consent. One fact shapes the design: every function aligns the firm’s separate views, and a firm whose views have converged shares its blind spots, so in a slow-feedback, ruin-exposed environment an aligning system can manufacture the correlated error it was built to prevent.  [AI Disclosure: Claude was utilized during the drafting phase for text editing, grammatical corrections, and stylistic improvements. The final analysis, insights, and conclusions remain exclusively the work of the authors.]

title: Contribution to the EDPB Public Consultation 1/2026 'Guidelines 1/2026 on Processing of Personal Data for Scientific Research Purposes'
affiliations: KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP), , KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP), KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP), affiliation not provided to SSRN, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Contribution to the EDPB Public Consultation 1/2026 'Guidelines 1/2026 on Processing of Personal Data for Scientific Research Purposes'
detail.abstract:
The EDPB’s Draft Guidelines on processing for scientific research purposes form an important milestone in clarifying how the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) operates in a research context. We welcome the Draft Guidelines and the clarifications on many important aspects that they provide. Still, coming from the perspective of researchers actively involved in many cross-disciplinary research projects, we find that the Draft Guidelines could be clearer on some aspects, while other issues we encountered in our research are not yet addressed.

With this contribution to the public consultation, we aim to assist the EDPB in further finetuning the final version of their guidance by listing (i) issues we find in need of clarification; and (ii) open questions that could be addressed. Our comments are focused on four aspects of the Draft Guidelines: (1) aspects concerning the scope of application of the guidelines; (2) questions around the proposed conceptualisation of scientific research; (3) clarifications for the appropriate safeguards in the context of Article 89 GDPR; (4) clarifications regarding the conceptualisation of biometric data in a research context; and (5) remarks on the processing of special categories of personal data for scientific research purposes.

title: Secure Cloud Evolution: A Mathematical Framework for Byzantine-Fault-Tolerant Multi-Generational Cloud Architectures
affiliations: Ibn Tofail University, Ibn Tofail University and Ibn Tofail University

detail.title: Secure Cloud Evolution: A Mathematical Framework for Byzantine-Fault-Tolerant Multi-Generational Cloud Architectures
detail.abstract: Cloud computing has evolved from centralized data centers to distributed multi-generational architectures spanning edge, fog, and quantum computing. This evolution introduces unprecedented security challenges, particularly regarding Byzantine faults. We propose Generational Byzantine Fault Tolerance (GBFT), a novel mathematical framework extending classical PBFT to accommodate heterogeneous cloud generations with varying trust assumptions, latency constraints, and computational capabilities. GBFT employs multi-layered consensus graphs and dynamic reputation scoring to ensure security, liveness, and safety across generational boundaries. We achieve O(N) communication complexity through threshold signature optimization while maintaining resilience against f < N/3 Byzantine nodes per generation. The framework is validated through TLA + formal specifications and experimental evaluation.

title: AI Geoeconomics: Allied Electricity and Secure Data Centers
affiliations: and University of Houston

detail.title: AI Geoeconomics: Allied Electricity and Secure Data Centers
detail.abstract: Global information power depends on more than just software; it requires secure physical foundations — AI compute and the electricity grids that power it. This manuscript argues that the U.S. risks ceding strategic advantage to China by neglecting the “Cloud-Grid Nexus.” With PRC-linked entities already positioned to potentially influence power grids and 147 power plants across Southeast Asia, a critical digital battleground, the threat of hardware-enabled espionage and coercion is acute. To counter this, the authors propose a “Datacenters and Dynamos” strategy. This geoeconomic framework advocates for integrated U.S. and allied export financing to deploy secure computing capacity alongside reliable power generation. By treating data centers and power grids as a unified security asset, Washington can work to ensure the global AI ecosystem runs on “allied rails,” preventing a repeat of the 5G infrastructure crisis and securing the physical layers of information power.

title: Endogenous Susceptibility in Markets for Repeated Extraction: A Behavioral-Industrial-Organization Model of a Self-Reinforcing Trap

detail.title: Endogenous Susceptibility in Markets for Repeated Extraction: A Behavioral-Industrial-Organization Model of a Self-Reinforcing Trap

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for conducting this study.

detail.abstract: High-cost consumer credit-payday loans, overdraft, buy-now-pay-later-keeps the same borrowers returning cycle after cycle, with a large share of loans concentrated in long repeat sequences. This paper offers a behavioral-industrial-organization account of why. It closes a loop two literatures leave open: behavioral IO shows firms exploit consumer biases but treats each bias as fixed, while the psychology of scarcity shows hardship degrades decisions but contains no firms. Here susceptibility to exploitation rises with financial scarcity, a firm targets it, and the extraction deepens scarcity. Micro-founding the susceptibility channel from a cognitive-bandwidth budget makes its curvature a theoretical object, and a behavioral poverty trap arises exactly when a safe basin coexists with a feedback peak that beats recovery. The trap is bistable and hysteretic: temporary targeting causes permanent entrapment. Under income risk it becomes a trapping hazard with a closedform escape law, verified against simulation. A monopolist's optimal policy is harvest-then-rest; competition raises aggregate targeting and can spring a trap a monopolist would avoid-though that competition can lower welfare for behaviorally vulnerable consumers is itself established, and the contribution here is its dynamic, endogenous-vulnerability form. The trap is regressive, and because it is irreversible, optimal regulation is preventive. Calibrated to standard parameters, the model reproduces the CFPB's payday-lending moments-the heavy-tailed loan-sequence distribution, nonamortization, and regressivity-that a no-feedback benchmark cannot. The premise that scarcity raises bias is empirically contested, so the theory is framed conditionally, with a testable bimodal signature.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography for Cloud: A Mathematical Migration Framework for the Q-Day Era
affiliations: Ibn Tofail University, Ibn Tofail University and Ibn Tofail University

detail.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography for Cloud: A Mathematical Migration Framework for the Q-Day Era
detail.abstract: The advent of quantum computing poses an existential threat to classical cryptography, with RSA-2048 potentially breakable within 15 years and breakout times for AI-driven attacks reduced to 27 seconds. This paper proposes PQC-Cloud (PQC-Cloud), a mathematical framework for migrating cloud infrastructures to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards. We formalize the Mosca Migration Theorem for risk assessment, introduce Hybrid Cryptographic Transition (HCT) combining classical and post-quantum algorithms, and present Lattice-Based Cloud Encryption (LBCE) using NIST-standardized ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Our framework achieves 1,600-byte overhead per TLS handshake and 80-150 microseconds additional latency, validated through formal verification and real-world deployment across AWS, Azure, and GCP multi-cloud environments.

title: A Modular AI Framework for Financial Cybercrime Investigation Across Legal Jurisdictions

detail.title: A Modular AI Framework for Financial Cybercrime Investigation Across Legal Jurisdictions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Financial cybercrime has grown increasingly sophisticated, operating across organizational, state, federal, and international boundaries. Investigators must analyze large volumes of financial transactions, digital evidence, communication records, and multi-source intelligence while navigating diverse legal frameworks. Although artificial intelligence has advanced fraud detection, anomaly detection, and criminal network analysis, most existing AI solutions are built for specific datasets, organizations, or legal jurisdictions, which makes them difficult to reuse, adapt, or scale across investigative environments. We argue that this limitation is not primarily a data problem but an architectural one: legal knowledge is entangled with investigative logic, and that entanglement is what prevents portability. This paper proposes a Modular AI Framework for Financial Cybercrime Investigation Across Legal Jurisdictions that separates reusable investigative capabilities from jurisdiction-specific legal knowledge. Core components include data ingestion, entity resolution, knowledge-graph construction, criminal-network reconstruction, evidence correlation, AI-assisted reasoning, and explainable decision support, while all jurisdictionspecific rules are isolated in a dedicated Legal Knowledge Layer and applied across the functional modules at runtime. The same investigative workflow can then adapt to a new statutory or regulatory environment by replacing the Legal Knowledge Layer rather than redesigning the analytical core, improving portability, maintainability, and long-term adaptability across state, federal, and international systems. Following a Design Science Research methodology, we present a conceptual reference architecture, demonstrate the framework using an illustrative multi-jurisdiction scenario, and discuss how the framework may support explainable, governed, and human-centered investigations. The paper establishes a foundation for future implementation, empirical validation, and adaptation across diverse legal jurisdictions and financial-crime domains.

title: Verified Ownership, Unverified Trust: The Effect of Digital asset Disclosure on Followership Expansion
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Supply Chain & Information Systems, University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee - Sheldon B. Lubar School of Business, City University of NY, Baruch College, Zicklin School of Business and University of Miami Herbert Business School

detail.title: Verified Ownership, Unverified Trust: The Effect of Digital asset Disclosure on Followership Expansion
detail.abstract: Self-presentation in online social networks is constrained by a fundamental credibility problem: users can easily fabricate claims about their expertise, status, or affiliations. The emergence of blockchain-enabled digital asset disclosure changes this dynamic by allowing users to publicly verify ownership in a way that is financially costly, technically binding, and difficult to fake. Drawing from signaling theory, we argue that this verified form of disclosure represents a substantially stronger signal than those examined in prior IS research, and we examine whether and how it affects followership expansion. We find that digital asset disclosure significantly increases subsequent followership expansion, but this effect is not uniform. Once prior domain history is taken into account, the benefit of disclosure is concentrated among users with richer pre-treatment NFT trading histories. Additionally, we show that the disclosure effect operates partly through perceived competence, whereas we find no corresponding evidence for perceived reliability. Leveraging Twitter's rollout of verified NFT profile pictures, we test these arguments using propensity score matching with a two-way fixed effects difference-indifferences framework. Our study contributes to IS research on platform-mediated disclosure and to signaling theory and credibility research in online environments.

title: A Theory of Money as a Network Good
affiliations: Stanford University

detail.title: A Theory of Money as a Network Good
detail.abstract: I develop a theory of money as a network good, micro-founding the value of monetary assets from bilateral trade primitives on a random graph. An asset achieves monetary status when its acceptance by trading partners generates sufficient network externalities to sustain a universal acceptance equilibrium. The stability of that equilibrium depends on the degree of heterogeneity in the trading network: more concentrated networks with high-degree hubs are more likely to tip into universal acceptance and harder to dislodge once there. The network premium on monetary assets (the convenience yield) is derived as a theorem from first principles rather than assumed, and maps directly to empirical measures of the Treasury convenience yield. The model exhibits a sharp phase transition: monetary status is a discrete state, not a matter of degree, generating discontinuous convenience yields, endogenous hysteresis, and excess volatility near the tipping threshold. I apply the framework to four phenomena: dollarization and its persistence, dollar dominance, monetary union and optimal currency areas, and safe asset shortages.

title: Governing the Unpredictable: A Layered Reference Architecture for AI Systems Deployment in Enterprise and Regulated Environments
affiliations: Claremont Graduate University

detail.title: Governing the Unpredictable: A Layered Reference Architecture for AI Systems Deployment in Enterprise and Regulated Environments
detail.abstract: Enterprise investment in articial intelligence continues to accelerate, yet a recurring observation across industry analyses is that a large share of AI initiatives do not transition from pilot programs to sustained operational deployment. Reported estimates vary widely by source and denition, but converge on the qualitative nding that most enterprise AI eorts stall before reaching durable production use. Prevailing explanations focus on model performance, data quality, or talent shortages. This paper advances a dierent thesis: a primary failure mode is architectural. Organizations lack coherent control structures capable of integrating probabilistic AI systems into the deterministic governance environments that enterprise and regulated contexts require. To address this gap, this study develops and preliminarily examines the AI Controls Framework, a seven-layer reference architecture for AI deployment in enterprise and regulated environments. Conceptually inspired by the Open Systems Interconnection model for networking and the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture for industrial control, the framework denes discrete layers spanning systems of record, connectivity and access control, data processing and context, workow orchestration, policy and governance, delivery and embedding, and observability and continuous improvement. A central design choice distinguishes this framework from existing approaches: governance is treated not as external oversight applied after technical deployment, but as an architectural primitive embedded structurally throughout all layers from inception. The study employs a qualitative, multi-method design combining grounded theory development with comparative case study analysis. Data collection includes 56 semi-structured interviews with AI practitioners, executives, and governance stakeholders across nancial services, federal government, manufacturing, and healthcare, plus architectural analysis of 11 enterprise AI deployments. Within this sample, deployment diculties mapped systematically to weaknesses in identiable architectural layers rather than to random implementation deciencies. Of the failures coded across the case material, most were attributed, on interpretive coding, to specic layer inadequacies, with the upper socio-technical layers governing delivery, policy, and observability accounting for the largest share of primary failure events. Architectural completeness appeared associated with deployment outcomes across the cases examined, a pattern that should be interpreted cautiously given the exploratory, within-sample design. The AI Controls Framework contributes to IT governance and management control scholarship by proposing a reference architecture specically designed for AI deployment, extending socio-technical systems theory to probabilistic technical components operating within deterministic organizational structures, and providing practitioners with a diagnostic and design model intended to help organizations reduce deployment risk, accelerate time-to-value, and institutionalize AI as core operating infrastructure.

title: Internationalisation Strategies of European Energy Management Firms in Emerging Markets: An Exploratory Analysis of the Turkish Case
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Internationalisation Strategies of European Energy Management Firms in Emerging Markets: An Exploratory Analysis of the Turkish Case
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the conditions under which European energy management firms can establish a durable strategic position in emerging economies, using Türkiye as an exploratory case. Drawing on internationalisation theory and strategic-management frameworks, it analyses how digital energy solutions — energy management systems (EMS), demand-response mechanisms and carbon-compliance services — interact with the institutional, regulatory and industrial dynamics of a rapidly growing economy facing intensifying decarbonisation pressures.

The study employs a qualitative, exploratory methodology combining documentary analysis, regulatory monitoring and established strategic frameworks (PESTEL analysis, the VRIO model and internationalisation theories). Rather than relying on primary field data, it develops a structured interpretive reading of market conditions and institutional dynamics.

The analysis suggests that Türkiye's industrial intensity, energy dependency and exposure to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) generate significant demand for digital energy management solutions, while regulatory complexity, institutional fragmentation and uneven industrial readiness constrain market entry. The findings underline the analytical importance of modular, cost-efficient and locally adaptable solutions, alongside phased entry logics grounded in regional prioritisation, pilot projects in organised industrial zones and partnerships with local stakeholders.

The paper contributes to the literature on energy-transition technologies and the internationalisation of clean-tech firms by proposing an exploratory analytical framework for understanding how energy management firms position themselves in structurally complex emerging markets.

title: Cooperative Multi-Device Neural Network Intelligence System Via Inference Partitioning in a C#/.NET Framework

detail.abstract: Contemporary artificial intelligence systems remain predominantly dependent on centralized cloud infrastructures. These dependencies introduce substantial latency, cost overhead, and an inflexible reliance on persistent network connectivity. Similarly, individual edge devices-smartphones or embedded systems lack the memory and computational capacity to execute large-scale neural networks independently. This paper presents NightFrame, a cooperative multidevice neural network intelligence system that addresses these dual constraints through capability-aware mesh orchestration and tensor-level inference partitioning, implemented entirely within a C#/.NET ecosystem. The proposed architecture decomposes a centrally orchestrated neural network workload into granular shards, which are then distributed across a heterogeneous mesh of edge devices, where each node is dynamically assigned computational responsibilities proportional to its real-time hardware profile. Core C# system services, including and not limited to the Orchestra-torService, ShardCoordinator, DroneRegistry, and LedgerService, are constructed as independently scalable micro-services communicating via gRPC and SignalR. This demonstrates a robust distributed AI orchestration that is achievable using standard enterprise tooling outside of traditional Python-centric machine learning environments. To establish trust and incentivize honest participation within the decentralized mesh, we introduce a theoretical cryptographic consensus protocol coupled with a tokenized credit ledger that records, verifies, and rewards node contributions within the form of a digital economy checking/balancing system. We also present companion user interfaces spanning web (Next.js), mobile (React Native/Expo), and desktop (WinForms/WPF) platforms for real-time mesh telemetry, prompt submission, and administrative oversight of the overall product architecture. Although the current implementation remains a research prototype, the networking foundation, cellular telemetry aggregation, and economic ledger infrastructures have been successfully demonstrated in this paper. This working paper establishes a practical blueprint for transitioning artificial intelligence processing from siloed, cloud-dependent paradigms to resilient, privacy-preserving, and horizontally scalable cooperative edge intelligence networks.

title: Multinational Joint Capabilities in the Americas: How the US Marine Corps Force Design 2030 can Pave the Way for Collective Defense

detail.abstract: This article examines how the U.S. Marine Corps Force Design 2030 concept can inform stronger multinational joint capabilities and collective defense in the Americas. In this context, the article presents Force Design 2030 as a useful framework for improving interoperability, joint training, shared platforms, and coordinated maritime and amphibious capabilities across regional partners. It also highlights the limits of existing defense arrangements, including budget constraints, doctrinal differences, and the absence of a comprehensive hemispheric defense concept. The article concludes that Latin American naval and marine forces could benefit from adapting elements of Force Design 2030, especially distributed operations, maritime-centric planning, and multidomain integration, to support a more flexible and cooperative approach to hemispheric security.

title: Making the Plan the Bad Guy: How Socio-Technical Artifacts Depersonalize Accountability in Software Teams
affiliations: and Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT)

detail.title: Making the Plan the Bad Guy: How Socio-Technical Artifacts Depersonalize Accountability in Software Teams
detail.abstract: Organizational accountability for failure is usually treated as an interpersonal accomplishment: managers assign it, colleagues confer or withhold it, leaders make a team feel safe to admit mistakes. We ask how material artifacts participate in this work. Through a field study of five software development teams in the years following their adoption of agile practices, we show that socio-technical artifacts (automated test suites, continuous integration systems, and visible workflow walls) materially carry and enact accountability relationships rather than merely supporting them. We develop the idea of depersonalized accountability: as teams build these artifacts into their work, the artifacts take over the interpersonally costly roles of holding people to account, the messenger who delivers unwelcome news, the accuser who attributes failure, the judge who rules on what counts, so that no colleague has to be the one who confronts, points, or rules. The attribution of failure, and even the discomfort of it, may remain, but the human accuser does not. That is what lowers the interpersonal stakes of experimenting, integrating unfinished work, and surfacing problems, continuously and impersonally rather than through a leader's ongoing behavior. We theorize this as a cycle in which artifacts and relational conditions are mutually constituted, and specify when the same artifacts instead intensify surveillance and defensive silence. Our account extends sociomaterial theory beyond cognition and coordination to the felt experience of accountability and safety, and reframes psychological safety as one outcome of a material process rather than a purely social achievement.

title: Sandboxes, Safe Harbors, and Sunset Clauses: Designing Adaptive Regulation for AI that Doesn't become Obsolete on Arrival

detail.title: Sandboxes, Safe Harbors, and Sunset Clauses: Designing Adaptive Regulation for AI that Doesn't become Obsolete on Arrival
detail.abstract: Traditional regulatory approaches-statute-based, prescriptive, and slow to update-are structurally mismatched with the pace of artificial intelligence development. The European Union's AI Act was first proposed in April 2021 and formally adopted in March 2024; during those three years, the technology landscape it was designed to govern was transformed by GPT-4, open-source foundation models, AI agents, and multimodal systems that the original proposal did not contemplate. This temporal mismatch is not a failure of legislative process-it is a structural characteristic of statute-based regulation applied to exponentially advancing technology. This paper argues that effective AI regulation must be inherently adaptive-designed to learn, evolve, and self-correct at a pace compatible with technological change-and examines three institutional mechanisms borrowed from fintech and telecom regulation: regulatory sandboxes (controlled environments where innovators can test AI applications under regulatory supervision with temporary compliance exemptions), safe harbors (legal protections for organizations that follow specified governance best practices), and sunset clauses (mandatory review and reauthorization periods that force periodic reassessment of regulatory relevance). Drawing on case evidence from the UK Financial Conduct Authority's fintech sandbox, Singapore's AI Verify governance framework, India's telecom licensing evolution, and the EU AI Act's sandbox provisions, the paper introduces the Adaptive AI Regulation Model (AARM)-an integrated regulatory lifecycle framework that combines all three mechanisms into a continuous learning loop: sandbox (learn from real deployment) → safe harbor (incentivize voluntary governance) → statute with sunset (mandate with built-in expiration and review). The central argument is that regulatory durability in AI comes not from getting the rules right the first time but from building institutional capacity for continuous regulatory learning. The paper concludes with implications for regulators and policymakers designing AI governance frameworks, industry association leaders engaging with regulatory processes, legal scholars studying regulatory design, and government affairs teams in technology companies advocating for adaptive regulatory mechanisms.

title: eXtended Interactive Education (XIE): House-Based Gamification, Cross-Batch Competition, and the Psychology of Reward-Driven Learning
affiliations: SIN education and Technology Private Limited

detail.title: eXtended Interactive Education (XIE): House-Based Gamification, Cross-Batch Competition, and the Psychology of Reward-Driven Learning

detail.abstract:
Standard classroom design removes three things that make people work hard: immediate feedback, visible competition, and collective accountability. eXtended Interactive Education (XIE) is a framework that puts them back. The experiment described here was run by SIN School of AI at Lucky Institute of Professional Studies, Jodhpur, across 200 students split into two batches. Both batches ran the same gamified structure: four houses (Gryffindor, Ravenclaw, Hufflepuff, Slytherin) with character-based academic identities, a unified points bank, and one shared leaderboard visible to all 200 students simultaneously. No batch had an advantage in content or instruction.
What emerged was a mutual monitoring dynamic we did not explicitly design: each batch watched the other batch's house standings without being told to, and adjusted effort accordingly. Attendance stayed high. Voluntary practice increased. Students began self-identifying by house within the first week. Confidence scores rose in both batches, most sharply after visible rank improvements. A replication across approximately 180 students at JIET Universe, Jodhpur produced similar patterns. This paper documents the design, mechanism, and outcomes — and proposes XIE as replicable infrastructure for any programme that wants engagement without external enforcement.

title: MACROCAST: A Vintage-Consistent Time Series Foundation Model for Real-Time Macroeconomic Forecasting
affiliations: Brandeis University - International Business School, Queen Mary, University of London and Brandeis University - International Business School

detail.title: MACROCAST: A Vintage-Consistent Time Series Foundation Model for Real-Time Macroeconomic Forecasting
detail.abstract: We introduce MACROCAST, a lightweight Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) for real-time macroeconomic forecasting. Existing TSFMs suffer from data leakage in two forms: temporal contamination, as the model may have seen the realized values of the series it forecasts, and revision bias, as training on fully revised data diverges from the preliminary, vintage-specific releases available to real-time forecasters. MACROCAST is, to our knowledge, the first TSFM that rules out both forms of leakage entirely: at no stage of training is the model exposed to information that would not have been available to a forecaster in real time. We train MACROCAST first on purely synthetic time series in approximately one GPU-day and then fine-tune it on synthetic time series drawn from Bayesian VARs, dynamic factor models, and ARIMA specifications estimated on vintage-specific ALFRED data. Because pretraining uses only simulated data and fine-tuning uses only real-time vintages, no observed future or revised value ever enters the model; each fine-tuning run takes nine minutes. Evaluated on the FRED-MD database in a genuine real-time out-of-sample exercise, MACROCAST improves on the AR(1) benchmark for roughly 80% of series-horizon pairs, matches or surpasses Chronos-2, the strongest currently available TSFM, and outperforms the Bayesian VAR and dynamic factor model benchmarks, all in a data-leakage-free manner.

title: Product Architecture and Reputation: Evidence from Second Wines
affiliations: Imperial College London

detail.title: Product Architecture and Reputation: Evidence from Second Wines
detail.abstract: I show that product architecture shapes how reputation is capitalized and formed. Exploiting hand-collected information on second wines, I find that expert ratings are capitalized less strongly into the prices of second wines than into those of first wines, yet ratings of second wines positively predict future first-wine prices. These positive spillovers provide evidence of collective and upward reputation formation across vertically linked products and are not readily explained by reverse spillovers or horizontal differentiation. I also document a convex relationship between ratings and prices, suggesting that elite wineries have particularly strong incentives to produce second wines.

title: India's AI Policy Vacuum: between Digital Public Infrastructure Ambition and Governance Readiness

detail.title: India's AI Policy Vacuum: between Digital Public Infrastructure Ambition and Governance Readiness
detail.abstract: India occupies a paradoxical position in the global artificial intelligence landscape: it is simultaneously the world's largest source of AI engineering talent (producing approximately 30-35% of the global supply of ML engineers and data scientists), a massive domestic market for AI deployment (1.4 billion potential users across a rapidly digitizing economy), an ambitious builder of population-scale digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar's 1.3 billion identities, UPI's 10+ billion monthly transactions, ONDC's open commerce network), and a significant laggard in AI-specific governance. The IndiaAI Mission commits substantial public investment to sovereign compute infrastructure, indigenous foundation models, and AI skilling-yet India has no binding AI regulation, no sector-specific AI governance standards, and a Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) that addresses data privacy without specifically governing the AI systems that process that data. This paper examines this governance vacuum through three analytical lenses: the deployment gap (AI systems operating at population scale without regulatory guardrails in lending, hiring, healthcare, and law enforcement), the institutional gap (absence of the specialized agencies, technical expertise, and enforcement mechanisms required to implement AI governance), and the strategic tension (political incentives to delay regulation that might slow AI adoption, even as governance failures accumulate at scale). The paper introduces the India AI Governance Maturity Model (IAGMM)-a three-phase governance roadmap that sequences institutional capacity building (2026-2028), sector-specific standards (2028-2030), and cross-cutting legislation (2030-2032) in a way that supports rather than constrains India's AI ambitions. The paper argues that India's governance vacuum is not merely a regulatory delay but a strategic risk that threatens the sustainability, credibility, and international legitimacy of India's AI growth trajectory. The paper concludes with implications for Indian policymakers, industry bodies (NASSCOM, iSPIRT), global enterprises deploying AI in India, development organizations, and comparative governance researchers.

title: On The “Delawarization of Bankruptcy” Debate
affiliations: New York University School of Law and George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: On The “Delawarization of Bankruptcy” Debate
detail.abstract:
In the early 1990s, the Delaware bankruptcy court replaced the Southern District of New York as the preferred venue for large corporate bankruptcies. This new phenomenon has drawn the attention of the National Bankruptcy Review Commission, the United States Congress, and numerous legal commentators. Although many of the people drawing attention to the Delawarization of bankruptcy are doing so because they have lost business for example, bankruptcy lawyers in other jurisdictions-or influence-for example, bankruptcy judges in other jurisdictions-as a result of the migration, there appears to be a legitimate, non-pecuniary concern that something is amiss and that justice is being denied. The leading critics, Lynn LoPucki along with his co-authors Ted Eisenberg, Sara Kalin, and Joseph Doherty, have denounced this development as, in the words of Eisenberg and LoPucki, an “embarrassing pattern of forum shopping.” Other commentators, including Douglas Baird, Robert Rasmussen, Randal Thomas, Kenneth Ayotte, and David Skeel, present “forum shopping” not as an embarrassment, but as part of beneficial jurisdictional competition that serves to force bankruptcy judges to make bankruptcy outcomes more efficient. Both camps cannot be correct, but both can be wrong.

The arguments for and against the phenomenon known as the Delawarization of bankruptcy presuppose that the phenomenon is an important one, good or bad. It is not certain, however, that the Delawarization of bankruptcy is even a significant event, much less a sustainable one. We offer a conjecture that the apparent dominance of Delaware as a bankruptcy venue is a merely apparent dominance, with in fact few firms strongly preferring Delaware to their local jurisdictions. We also question whether the evidence offered for or against jurisdictional competition in bankruptcy is persuasive or even joins issue with the other side. We observe further that, in any case, the market for bankruptcy filings has not yet exhibited the long-term stability that marks Delaware's dominance in the market for corporate charters, and thus may not deserve the attention it has received.

In this Article, we present a selective critique of the debate concerning the Delawarization of bankruptcy. In Part I, we summarize the competing perspectives on the value of competition in the market for bankruptcy filings. In Part II, we consider whether there is any evidence of competition for bankruptcy filings, or of Delaware's dominance assuming such competition. We also consider whether the proponents or opponents of such competition offer evidence that conflicts with rather than complements the other side. In Part III, we address, and find wanting, the analogy between Delaware's attraction as a bankruptcy jurisdiction and Delaware's attraction as a charter jurisdiction. Finally, we conclude that it may be premature either to praise or to condemn Delaware as a jurisdiction for bankruptcy reorganization.

title: Does ESG-Motivated Stakeholder Pressure Work? Evidence from Environmental Violations
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business, Xi’an Jiaotong University, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics & Finance, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and Macquarie University

detail.title: Does ESG-Motivated Stakeholder Pressure Work? Evidence from Environmental Violations
detail.abstract: We document a major shift in the effectiveness of stakeholder pressure in disciplining firms for poor environmental performance. Before 2007, stakeholder reactions to firms' environmental violations had negligible valuation effects. Since 2007, however, stakeholder reactions have imposed large and increasing costs on polluting firms. Relative to matched peers, violators suffer outflows of ESG-oriented investors, higher costs of capital, and a decline in sales. Firms respond by rebuilding their reputations through new ESG-related board committees and reduced greenhouse gas emissions. These results indicate that stakeholder pressure has become value-relevant for polluting firms only recently, a shift that coincides with the 2006 launch of the U.N. Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and the emergence of largescale SRI fund flows.
