title: Who Speaks for the Affected? The Missing Stakeholder Problem in AI Policy Consultations

detail.title: Who Speaks for the Affected? The Missing Stakeholder Problem in AI Policy Consultations
detail.abstract: AI policy consultations-public comment periods, expert panels, multi-stakeholder forums, and parliamentary hearings-systematically underrepresent the populations most directly affected by algorithmic deployment. This paper documents the structural exclusion of affected populations from AI governance processes across the United States, European Union, and India by identifying four mechanisms of exclusion: (1) technical jargon barriers that render participation inaccessible to non-expert publics; (2) comment period architectures that privilege organized industry and civil society actors over individual affected parties; (3) geographic and economic barriers to in-person consultation in national capitals; and (4) fundamental information asymmetries between AI deployers who understand system design and affected populations who experience consequences without comprehending causes. Drawing on democratic theory, procedural justice scholarship, and empirical analysis of consultation submissions across 14 regulatory proceedings, the paper introduces the Consultation Exclusion Framework (CEF)-a four-mechanism model explaining why affected populations are structurally absent from AI governance-and proposes the Participatory Remedy Architecture (PRA), a five-component structural reform package. The paper argues that without structural reform, AI governance risks becoming a professionally mediated conversation about populations rather than with them, undermining both democratic legitimacy and regulatory effectiveness.

title: Antitrust as Antidiscrimination: Competition Law Remedies Against Gender Wage Discrimination
affiliations: and Faculty of Law, University of Oxford

detail.title: Antitrust as Antidiscrimination: Competition Law Remedies Against Gender Wage Discrimination
detail.abstract: In recent years, competition authorities across the world have departed from their historical reluctance to engage with labour markets and are increasingly focusing on limiting the ability of employers to exploit workers in their pursuit of profits. While the ongoing debates on the application of competition law to labour markets have largely concentrated on the ability of employers to suppress wages and impose onerous terms on workers either unilaterally or through concerted action, the potential of monopsonistic employers to engage in wage discrimination among different categories of employees has received little academic attention. Building on the extensive economic literature on gender wage disparity and monopsonistic discrimination, this article demonstrates how employers enjoying market power are able to exploit socio-economic constraints on women’s labour mobility to remunerate them less than male counterparts. It argues that such monopsonistic wage discrimination constitutes a violation of EU competition law, and as such, competition law should complement constitutional guarantees and labour legislation as part of a broader regulatory framework to promote gender wage equality.

title: Water Stress, Agricultural Exposure, and Banking Fragility: Evidence from Tunisian Governorates
affiliations: Ecole Superieure des Sciences Economiques et Commerciales de Tunis (ESSECT),  Université de Tunis

detail.title: Water Stress, Agricultural Exposure, and Banking Fragility: Evidence from Tunisian Governorates
detail.abstract: This paper examines how hydrological stress propagates into banking sector fragility through the agricultural credit channel in a climate-vulnerable emerging economy. Using a novel governorate-level panel dataset covering Tunisia over the period 2003-2023, we estimate a two-way fixed effects model that interacts a water stress index with local agricultural employment intensity. We provide the first sub-national evidence showing that the impact of water stress on agricultural non-performing loans (NPLs) is significantly amplified in regions with greater agricultural dependence. The estimated interaction effect is large, robust across specifications, and economically meaningful. We further document a non-linear relationship characterized by a threshold beyond which the marginal effect attenuates, consistent with endogenous credit rationing. Dynamic specifications reveal strong persistence in NPLs, implying a substantial long-run amplification of climate-related shocks. Importantly, we identify a structural break following the 2011 revolution, suggesting that institutional reforms and public credit programs significantly mitigated the transmission of water stress into banking risk in the subsequent period. Our findings contribute to the climate-finance literature by highlighting the importance of sectoral exposure and regional heterogeneity in shaping financial vulnerability to physical climate risk. They also carry direct implications for climate stress testing, macroprudential regulation, and the design of agricultural risk-sharing mechanisms in water-scarce economies.

detail.abstract:
Reports about misconduct in the financial sector are seemingly endless. Misconduct is wide-ranging and varied—from abusive practices in mortgage securities and commodities markets to manipulation of foreign exchange and interest rates.2 Truly, the reports suggest an ethical crisis in finance. A major complaint is about the lack of serious efforts to hold to account executives that engaged in misconduct or were in leadership positions at the banks. The events call into question the adequacy of the current arrangements for ensuring integrity in the financial sector, at the institutional and individual levels.

This paper examines developments in the financial sector and identifies a role for regulatory ethics in promoting integrity and accountability. In this effort, the paper also explores theoretical perspectives in ethics and how they can shape business behavior. Specifically, the article proposes corporate codes of ethics, a mandatory requirement under the New York Stock Exchange Listing Rules, as instruments to promote morality in corporate conduct. Ethics codes, which are internally generated, must be tailored to reflect the experience and made more effective. They can be amplified to specify standards to govern the fiduciary duty of care applicable to executives, personal integrity and accountability. This method can be effective in shaping the moral climate in corporations and in checking misconduct.c

title: The New Post Roads The Postal Clause as an Affirmative Power to Provide Universal Internet Access

detail.title: The New Post Roads The Postal Clause as an Affirmative Power to Provide Universal Internet Access
detail.abstract: This Article argues that the Post Roads Clause-Congress's power "To establish Post Offices and post Roads"-is best understood as an affirmative grant of power to provide the nation's communicative infrastructure, and that the internet is the present-day object of that power. So understood, the clause supplies a constitutional warrant for a federal commitment to universal internet access. In making this argument, the Article departs from the dominant scholarly use of postal history. Anuj Desai has shown how early postal policy generated modern First and Fourth Amendment doctrine, treating the post office as a source of individual rights and constraints on government; this Article instead reads the same clause as a source of affirmative federal power to build and guarantee the channel itself. It also builds on Robert Natelson's originalist account of the clause-under which "establishing" a post road historically included constructing it-to defeat, on originalist grounds, the long-standing objection that the postal power permits only the designation of existing routes. The Article then synthesizes three doctrinal sources-the enumerated postal power read through its purpose, the implied-powers reasoning of McCulloch v. Maryland, and the Commerce Clause-into a single affirmative-provisioning theory, and distinguishes that theory from the common-carriage and Title II frames that dominate broadband law. After developing the normative case, the Article engages the strongest objections, including the early Republic's internal-improvements debate, federalism, market efficiency, and the absence of a limiting principle, and argues that these constrain the form a federal commitment should take far more than they defeat its constitutional legitimacy.

title: An Economic Analysis of Decentralized Commerce Trust Mechanism Based on Feynman Diagram Model

detail.title: An Economic Analysis of Decentralized Commerce Trust Mechanism Based on Feynman Diagram Model
detail.abstract: Background: Centralized e-commerce platforms have resolved the trust problem in remote transactions through platform credit intermediation, but have created a new "trust black hole"-platforms can unilaterally modify rules, freeze funds, and abuse user data, leaving both merchants and buyers locked into the platform. Existing consortium blockchain solutions remain permissioned and fail to fundamentally resolve the trust issue. Research Question: How can we construct a programmable credit system that does not rely on any centralized platform, thereby rebuilding the physical foundation of commercial trust from an economic perspective? Methodology: This paper proposes the "Decentralized Commerce Feynman Diagram Model," introducing the formal methods of quantum field theory's Feynman diagrams into commercial transaction modeling. Through the creation and annihilation mechanisms of dNFT pairs (+/-credit quanta), local interaction vertices, and dual-world conservation laws, we establish a comprehensive trust cost analysis framework. Key Findings: 1. Trust Cost Quantification: The trust cost of remote transactions is 15-30% higher than face-to-face transactions (commissions 5-25% + return rates 10-30% + processing time 3-7 days). 2. Locality Value: Two local vertices (transaction contract + receipt contract) can reduce trust cost to $0.50/transaction (vs. platform commissions of 5-25%). 3. Game-Theoretic Stability: When delta x V_future >= V_fraud, honesty is the optimal strategy (empirical: at 96% discount factor, annual revenue $24,000 > fraud gain $5,000). 4. Cold-Start Feasibility: A three-dimensional initial credit generation mechanism (asset staking + verifiable credentials + guarantees) can provide new merchants with an initial credit score of 75 (out of 100). Policy Implications: Provides a theoretical basis for regulatory framework design, credit system standardization, and cross-border transaction trust mechanisms for decentralized commerce.

title: 'Rules-Based' Corporate Capitalism: Reading Bad Boy Billionaires-India as a Socio-legal Archive
affiliations: University of New England (Australia) - School of Law

detail.title: 'Rules-Based' Corporate Capitalism: Reading Bad Boy Billionaires-India as a Socio-legal Archive
detail.abstract: Across four emblematic episodes—Satyam Computer Services Ltd., Sahara India Corporation Ltd., Kingfisher Airlines Ltd., and Firestart Diamond Int. Ltd.—the paper traces how the state deploys categorisation and perimeter regulation (wilful defaulter, fugitive economic offender, personal guarantor) to re-centre control and accountability in corporate liability design. It argues that corporate scandals do not merely reveal private wrongdoing; they function as recurring stress tests of enforcement credibility in a promoter-led political economy where concentrated control persists alongside formal governance reforms. The article concludes that durable rules-based corporate capitalism depends less on spectacular enforcement and more on process-centred discipline, credible gatekeepers, investigatory capacity, civil remedy pathways and procedurally defensible reputational sanctions.

title: High-Drive Cognitive Configurations in Late-Modern Knowledge Societies: A Three-Loop Systems Model of Ambition, Isolation, and Risk

detail.title: High-Drive Cognitive Configurations in Late-Modern Knowledge Societies: A Three-Loop Systems Model of Ambition, Isolation, and Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the content of this paper. The research was conducted independently without external funding, commercial sponsorship, or institutional affiliation.

detail.abstract: Late-modern knowledge societies systematically reward cognitive performance, strategic ambition, and individual productivity, while often providing limited institutional structures for psychological integration or ethical constraint. Within this context, this paper introduces the High-Drive Cognitive Archetype (HDCA) as a conceptual model describing a recurrent configuration of elevated intelligence, sustained ambition, self-reliance, and progressive social isolation that emerges under meritocratic and hyper-competitive incentive structures. The paper makes three contributions. First, it reframes extreme ambition and high cognitive capacity not as fixed personality traits or clinical categories, but as system-conditioned outcomes shaped by the incentive architectures of contemporary knowledge economies. Second, it proposes a three-loop feedback framework-comprising a Performance-Reward Loop, an Isolation Loop, and a Self-Referential Loop-to explain how these conditions are both generated and self-reinforced within institutional environments lacking countervailing integrative mechanisms. Third, it argues that the associated risks should be interpreted primarily as institutional design externalities rather than individual moral or psychological failures, implying that mitigation requires structural redesign rather than behavioural attribution. Drawing on sociological theory, organisational psychology, and systems thinking, the paper analyses how high cognitive capacity and sustained ambition can simultaneously produce adaptive performance advantages and increased susceptibility to emotional detachment, moral disengagement, and high-risk decision orientation under conditions of social and institutional isolation. The HDCA is presented as a non-diagnostic analytical construct intended to support discussion of elite performance dynamics, leadership risk, and the unintended psychological consequences of meritocratic systems.

title: Regenerative Agentic Science How the Displaced Expert Becomes the Builder

detail.title: Regenerative Agentic Science How the Displaced Expert Becomes the Builder
detail.abstract: The marginal cost of turning subject-matter knowledge into working software is collapsing as capable AI coding agents absorb the execution of technical work. This paper argues that the same shift carries two faces: it displaces the routine, execution-bound roles that formed the lower rungs of knowledge work, and it unbundles domain expertise from coding skill, leaving expert judgment as the scarce and appreciating input. Drawing on recent labor-exposure estimates and an industry analysis of roughly 400,000 agentic coding sessions, the paper locates the binding constraint not in whether a system can be built but in whether someone with deep domain command owns its intent, its verification, and its governance. It introduces Regenerative Agentic Science as the discipline of building agents that regenerate a person's command of their field rather than substitute for it, and contrasts it deliberately with the prevailing meaning of agentic science, which centers machine autonomy and reduced human dependence. The paper specifies five commitments that distinguish regenerative from extractive agentic systems, illustrates the pattern across healthcare, law, finance, education, the skilled trades, operations, and agriculture, and states the conditions under which the thesis would fail, including the erosion of returns to expertise and capture by platforms.

title: Qualification and Expertise: The Detectable Signals of Professional Competence Distance

detail.title: Qualification and Expertise: The Detectable Signals of Professional Competence Distance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is self-represented in ongoing civil and administrative proceedings in Portugal concerning matters structurally similar to those discussed in this paper's companion application piece. The theoretical framework presented here was developed in part through that practical engagement and is offered in general form independent of any specific proceeding; no specific party, case, or jurisdiction is addressed in this paper. The author is also the founder of a commercial venture (KYC.co) whose broader product and policy work intersects with some of the institutional design concepts discussed here.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical and doctrinal legal analysis; it does not involve human subjects, personal data collection, or empirical research requiring ethics review.

detail.abstract: Institutions that allocate professional and expert roles — courts appointing technical experts, clients instructing lawyers, hospitals assigning clinicians, regulators approving auditors — routinely ask a single question: is this person qualified to do the work? In many institutional settings they ask a second, logically independent question only inconsistently or not at all: how close is this person's demonstrated experience to the specific matter at hand? That second question is not unknown to the law — it is, in substance, the question Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and the Daubert/Kumho Tire line of authority require a court to ask of expert testimony, and economists since Spence and Stiglitz have long treated credentials as an imperfect signal of ability rather than ability itself. What is missing, particularly in civil-law jurisdictions and in the routine allocation of counsel rather than expert witnesses, is a structured, ex ante way of asking it. This paper names the conflation of the two questions the Qualification–Expertise Fallacy, and argues that the gap it produces leaves a structured set of detectable signals — observable in a practitioner's career record, in an organisation's own departmental description of itself, and in the technical content of the matter assigned — capable of being measured and acted upon before a failure occurs rather than only litigated after one has. The paper develops three contributions, each narrower than a claim to conceptual originality and each, it argues, useful precisely because of that. First, it specifies semantic distance — the separation between a practitioner's demonstrated subject-matter experience and the technical content of a specific task — as an observable signal set, distinct from, and complementary to, the relational distance measured by network-proximity analysis, a separate and independently useful instrument addressed only briefly here. Second, it applies the standard law-and-economics model of the expected value of litigation, in which a disputed matter's value is discounted by the probability of a favourable outcome, to this signal set specifically: Realisable Resolution Value (RRV) frames competence distance as the variable principally responsible for that probability discount, giving it a structured and observable basis rather than leaving it to unstructured litigator judgment. Third, grounding both measures in settled doctrine rather than new theory, it connects the signal set to the existing law of agency, professional indemnity insurance, and vicarious and negligent-supervision liability, to explain why a competence failure in representation can generate liability running in as many as three directions — to the represented party, to the opposing party, and back to the institution that made the staffing decision — and why responsibility for that failure belongs, in the great majority of cases, to the institution rather than the individual practitioner. The paper illustrates the framework with a case study from an ongoing Portuguese proceeding and the output of a prototype measurement instrument, presented as a worked proofof-concept rather than as independent corroborating evidence, and closes with a proposal for how courts, regulators, firms, and insurers might act on these signals directly.

title: Where Estimators Are Exposed: State-Indexed Influence Geometry

detail.title: Where Estimators Are Exposed: State-Indexed Influence Geometry
detail.abstract: Standard errors aggregate influence across observations, obscuring how an estimator’s second-moment geometry varies across meaningful states and estimand directions. We develop state-indexed influence geometry, which compares conditional influence second moments with a reference moment. The resulting exposure surfaces identify where estimates draw empirical support, target episode-, overlap-, or region-year-specific audits, and, when paired with a valid covariance field, hypothesis, and alternative direction, characterize the noise underlying state-dependent power. Applications to local projections, treatment effects, and event studies reveal concentrated, direction-specific exposure and show how the method converts high-dimensional influence information into interpretable maps for empirical analysis.

title: The Fenton Distribution Solved: Closed-Form PDF, CDF, VaR, and ES for Sums of Correlated Lognormals

detail.title: The Fenton Distribution Solved: Closed-Form PDF, CDF, VaR, and ES for Sums of Correlated Lognormals
detail.abstract: The moment-based Latent representation of correlated lognormal sums (Nagy, 2026h) relies on scaled moments 𝑐𝑘 = 𝑚𝑘/𝑘! that grow as 𝑒 𝜎 2 max𝑘 2/2. This super-exponential growth is the root cause of ill-conditioning in the Padé resummation step: the moment Toeplitz matrix has condition number ∼ 𝑒𝑂(𝑁2 𝑃 ) , making the method impractical for 𝜎max > 0.8. The Smooth Latent Operator (Nagy, 2026j) mitigates this through regularization but cannot overcome the information-theoretic limit imposed by the growth rate. We show that the moments are the Latent representation of the wrong generating function. The moments are Taylor coefficients of the moment generating function 𝑀(𝑧) = 𝐸[𝑒𝑧𝑆], which has zero convergence radius for lognormal sums. By contrast, the Hermite-chaos expansion — the Wiener polynomial chaos of 𝑆 in the underlying Gaussian variables — has coefficients that decay factorially. This is because the exponential function 𝑒 𝑌 has a convergent Hermite series for 𝑌 ∼ 𝑁(𝜇, 𝜎2 ), with coefficients 𝜎 𝑘/𝑘!. The resulting Hermite Latent Λ 𝐻 = {𝑐𝐻 k } lives in ℓ 2 (no Gaussian weight needed), the characteristic function is recovered by a convergent inner product (no Padé resummation needed), and the CDF follows by Fourier-cosine inversion (Fang and Oosterlee, 2008). The entire chain is closed-form and well-conditioned for all 𝜎. We formalize this as a grade-3 Latent: the optimal choice of representation basis. The grade3 Latent for lognormal sums is the Hermite-chaos basis, selected by matching the basis to the problem’s generative structure (Gaussian → exponential → sum). The three-body problem’s use of Fourier coefficients (instead of Taylor coefficients) is the same grade-3 choice, matched to the problem’s periodic structure. The resulting CDF formula — a double finite sum of sines and cosines — is elementary in the Liouville-Risch sense: a finite composition of standard transcendental functions. By contrast, the normal CDF 𝑁(𝑥) is non-elementary (Liouville, 1835). The more complex distribution has the structurally simpler formula. This Elementariness Paradox is resolved by the grade-3 Latent: in the right coordinates, the lognormal sum is a trigonometric polynomial.

detail.abstract: Using an input-output (IO) framework, we assess the Iranian economy's structural exposure to the 2026 war involving Iran, the United States, and Israel, and the accompanying US naval blockade. Because realized data are unavailable, we measure the economic activity structurally tied to the disrupted sectors and trade flows, holding the production structure fixed. Drawing on the Central Bank of Iran's official 74-activity IO table for 2021/22, we propagate each shock in the direction its economics dictates. We apply the Ghosh inverse to assess war-related capacity losses in chemicals and basic metals and blocked imported intermediates; the Leontief inverse to trace the export blockade through upstream linkages; and the IO price model to measure cost pressure from disrupted imports. In aggregate, the episode implies exposure of 15.4 percent of gross output, 10.7 percent of value added, and 1.69 million job-equivalents, with output-weighted cost pressure of approximately 14.5 percent and a compensating-import requirement of roughly US$37 billion in foreign exchange. The results are driven primarily by war-related capacity losses and the two damaged sectors' network centrality, amplified by the blockade's compression of both intermediate-and final-goods trade. The disruption falls more heavily on investment than consumption and is robust to wide parameter variation.

title: Contaminated by Construction: Separating Simulation Noise from Model Risk in ES Backtests

detail.title: Contaminated by Construction: Separating Simulation Noise from Model Risk in ES Backtests
detail.abstract: Expected Shortfall backtesting under Basel III/IV suffers from an unmeasured structural weakness: Monte Carlo estimation of ES injects computational noise into the Acerbi-Székely (2014) test statistic, but the magnitude of this contamination has not been quantified. We prove that the test statistic’s variance decomposes additively as Varreturns + VarMC, separating the irreducible statistical uncertainty from the eliminable computational noise. This decomposition is the paper’s central result: it tells practitioners exactly how much of a backtest outcome is real and how much is Monte Carlo artifact. Simulation confirms that MC contributes roughly a third of total test variance at 𝑀 = 1,000 paths and 3–5% at 𝑀 = 10,000; the literature suggests contributions of up to 10% for heavier-tailed portfolios. For portfolios of correlated lognormal assets — covering the majority of linear equity and FX books — the MC component can be eliminated entirely using the Hermite-COS method, which computes ES, the CDF, and the density in closed form from Fourier coefficients. Setting VarMC = 0 yields 11–26% relative power gains and enables two qualitatively new tests: (i) a Probability Integral Transform test that detects distributional misspecifications invisible to any ES-only backtest; (ii) a tail likelihood ratio test that is optimal for simple tail alternatives by the Neyman-Pearson lemma. The algebraic chain from assumptions to conclusions is formally verified in Lean 4 (10 files, 53 lemmas, zero sorry; proof depth classified in Section 8.2a); probabilistic assumptions are supplied as hypotheses.

detail.abstract: Attributing crypto-asset activity to specific jurisdictions is not straightforward: transactions are pseudonymous, occur on platforms with global reach, and comparable cross-country data are scarce. This paper proposes a method to approximate such attribution from public exchange information, taking the fiat currency of each trading pair as a proxy for the jurisdiction. The approach yields two products per jurisdiction: an estimate of traded volumes by crypto-asset class, and a composition indicator — the share of stablecoins relative to unbacked crypto-assets. The dataset covers 28 fiat currencies across 18 centralized exchanges, with monthly data from January 2019 to March 2026. The data display an asymmetric pattern: in markets linked to emerging-market currencies, volumes concentrate in stablecoins, whereas in markets linked to advanced-economy currencies, unbacked crypto-assets retain a larger share — a regularity the author has termed asymmetric cryptoization. This is a proxy, not a census, with the limitations inherent to an opaque market and partial coverage; the results are a first approximation.

title: The Projected-Generator Method for Path-Dependent Derivative Pricing

detail.title: The Projected-Generator Method for Path-Dependent Derivative Pricing
detail.abstract: Derivative pricing has a clear mathematical target: compute the discounted risk-neutral value of a payoff under a specified model. For European vanilla contracts this target is often analytic or nearly analytic. The difficult cases are path-dependent derivatives — American and Bermudan exercise, barriers, autocallables, coupon memory, hit counts, and structured-product state — where standard methods rely on Monte Carlo simulation, regression continuation estimates, or high-dimensional PDE grids. This paper introduces projected-generator pricing as a finite-dimensional operator method for such contracts. Starting from the infinitesimal generator of the risk-neutral dynamics, the method projects the generator onto a finite basis and propagates continuation values by the resulting matrix semigroup. Path dependence is represented by finite event-state transitions around the same propagation primitive. American and Bermudan exercise become projected semigroup propagation plus pointwise exercise comparison plus re-projection, with no simulated-path regression. The contribution is a pricing architecture rather than a new isolated ingredient. Generator calculus, Galerkin projection, matrix exponentials, spectral bases, and Bellman recursion are combined into a deterministic engine for path-dependent derivatives. When the finite space is invariant under the generator, pricing is exact on that space; otherwise the projection residual measures approximation debt. For analytic payoffs under spectral bases the error decays exponentially, and Greeks are obtained by differentiating the same finite expansion rather than by bump-and-reprice. Benchmarks against Black-Scholes, COS, Longstaff-Schwartz, finite differences, Monte Carlo, and Merton jump-diffusion references show machine-precision European pricing, regression-free American pricing within 1% of published references, deterministic Greeks, finite-activity Poisson-jump support through a nonlocal Lévy generator, and a structured-product example priced without path simulation. The method is strongest when the model has a tractable generator, the path memory is finite state, and the effective dimension is low to moderate. High-dimensional baskets, rough volatility without a controlled lift, and severe discontinuities remain better served by Monte Carlo, finite differences, or adapted bases.

title: 'The Critical (Legal) Praxis of Costas Douzinas'

detail.title: 'The Critical (Legal) Praxis of Costas Douzinas'
detail.abstract: Douzinas’ work is made up of shards of critique that lacerate structures of power, legal orders, political regimes and economic apparatuses. Piecing these shards together does not give us a complete theory, but this chapter argues that it does contain a singular critical praxis. The chapter takes the ‘Oubliez Critique’ essay of 2005 as the centrepoint around which a praxis of critique emerges. There is no simple negation of the texts or themes under consideration, instead Douzinas begins by traversing the subject under consideration from within. The purpose of this traversal is not (or not simply) to disprove the argument, so much as exhausting the imminent possibilities of the text. In this exhaustion, new possibilities of emerge and these are understood by bringing existing critical theories to bear. From this exhaustion, the final move emerges, often in a nascent or gestural form, that is Douzinas’s critical praxis seeks to overcome and move beyond the structure or subject under consideration. The essay traces this critical praxis across Douzinas’ writings on human rights, legal theory and social movements.

title: Terminal Portfolio Value Distribution to Machine Precision

detail.title: Terminal Portfolio Value Distribution to Machine Precision
detail.abstract: We present a deterministic, semi-analytical framework for computing the complete distribution of a portfolio’s terminal value at horizon 𝑇 for correlated lognormal assets. Unlike traditional approaches, this method requires no Monte Carlo simulation. It directly yields the full probability density, the cumulative distribution, all moments, and exact quantile metrics such as loss Valueat-Risk (VaR) and loss Expected Shortfall (ES). The method is not closed-form in the classical sense (no finite elementary formula exists for the sum-of-lognormals distribution), but it achieves machine precision through a rapidly converging spectral scheme with controllable error. The method builds on the Hermite-COS representation (Nagy, 2026): the terminal portfolio value distribution is expressed as a finite trigonometric polynomial whose coefficients are computed from Gauss-Hermite quadrature over the correlation eigenstructure. The CDF is then a deterministic sine series, the PDF is a cosine series, the lower-tail terminal-value quantile is obtained by root-finding on the CDF, and the corresponding loss VaR and loss ES follow immediately from 𝐿𝑇 = 𝑆0−𝑆𝑇 . Both the quadrature and the spectral expansion converge exponentially, so with standard parameters (𝑄 = 40, 𝑁 = 128) the results match Monte Carlo to 4–5 significant figures — deterministically, in under one second. We demonstrate and validate the framework on three $100,000 portfolios spanning the practitioner landscape: 1. Bitcoin-heavy crypto portfolio (𝜎max = 90%, skewness = 3.6): extreme volatility where delta-normal underestimates the 1% loss by $128,000 — more than the portfolio itself. The Hermite-COS method matches Monte Carlo (5M paths) to within $53 on VaR. 2. Long-short equity hedge portfolio (net +40%, gross 200%): positions that can go negative. The method matches MC VaR 1% to within $10, natively handling short positions. 3. Diversified 60/40 multi-asset portfolio: the standard institutional setup. Matches MC VaR 1% to within $27, revealing $4,687 of hidden tail risk that the Gaussian assumption misses. All results are validated against Monte Carlo with 5 × 106 paths. Every risk measure agrees to 4–5 significant figures. The Hermite-COS computation completes in 0.4–0.8 seconds per portfolio and is perfectly deterministic: running the same portfolio twice always gives the same answer, unlike Monte Carlo where the VaR 1% fluctuates by $19–$21 between seeds.

title: Spectral Importance Sampling: Optimal Rare-Event Simulation via Eigenvalue-Conditioned Measure Change

detail.title: Spectral Importance Sampling: Optimal Rare-Event Simulation via Eigenvalue-Conditioned Measure Change
detail.abstract: Rare financial catastrophes are the events that matter most for risk management and the ones standard Monte Carlo handles worst: a one-in-a-million loss needs about a million samples to appear even once. Importance sampling addresses this by simulating under a tilted measure that makes rare events common and then correcting each sample by a likelihood ratio, but the central difficulty is choosing the tilt — in a portfolio of hundreds of correlated assets the space of tilts is vast and a poor choice increases variance rather than reducing it. This paper shows that the eigenvalue decomposition of the correlation matrix supplies a provably optimal tilting direction. The key structural fact is mode independence: the eigenvalue-weighted modes are mutually independent, so the measure change factorizes into independent per-mode exponential tilts, each with a closed-form saddle-point solution. The optimal tilt is computable in O(K) operations, independent of portfolio dimension. I establish three results. First, the factored estimator is unbiased and logarithmically efficient, with second moment bounded by C(l) times rho^(-2l), where rho > 1 is the analyticity radius of the portfolio characteristic function and l is the loss threshold. Second, the optimal per-mode tilt is the saddle point of the per-mode cumulant generating function, and the collection solves a separable convex program in the large-threshold regime. Third, there is a duality between the Bernstein ellipse radius governing spectral coefficient decay and the Cramer rate function governing tail probabilities, so the optimal importance-sampling domain coincides with the analyticity domain of the spectral representation. The variance reduction is exponential in the loss threshold for marginals with analytic characteristic functions and polynomial for heavy-tailed marginals (Student-t, Pareto, stable). I demonstrate the method on deep-tail VaR/ES estimation at the 10^-8 level, multi-asset barrier option pricing with correlated knock-out, and CDO tranche loss estimation under correlated defaults.

title: Reclaiming the Soul of Education: The Swiss Patriciates as a Model for Sustainable Learning and Societal Development
affiliations: The Swiss Institute for Alternative Thinking and The Swiss Institute for Alternative Thinking

detail.title: Reclaiming the Soul of Education: The Swiss Patriciates as a Model for Sustainable Learning and Societal Development
detail.abstract: In a world increasingly marked by disconnection—between individuals, between societies, and between humanity and nature—the necessity of reintegrating education with life itself becomes ever more pressing. The modern educational paradigm, often mechanised and detached from its environmental and communal roots, stands in stark contrast to models that have survived the test of time by embracing a holistic, nature-based, and community-driven approach to knowledge transmission. The Swiss Patriciates offer a striking case study of such a system. As an exemplary case integrating a variety of “devices suited for tackling international policy priorities in modern times, with a particular focus on the field of sustainability", they embody an educational ethos that seamlessly intertwines childhood development, communal stability, and environmental stewardship leading to befitting notions of responsibility and evolution on both the individual as well as collective level. Being a mode of organization that has community integration at its roots, it promotes individuals assuming responsibility themselves rather than being directed towards doing so, embodying a real hope- one that acts organically.  The bottom-up approach employed showcases the requirements for a foundation rooted in heritage that can drive healthy innovation that is in congruence with both inner and outer nature, and not just in accordance to a mental motto such as “progress”. This paper explores the relevance of this model to contemporary educational challenges and the ways in which it provides a pathway toward a more integrated, sustainable, and meaningful existence.

title: When Text Helps: AI Text Signals for Calibration-Sensitive Tail-Risk Decisions in Prediction Markets
affiliations: University of Waterloo - Department of Management Sciences and University of Waterloo - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: When Text Helps: AI Text Signals for Calibration-Sensitive Tail-Risk Decisions in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Prediction markets provide a demanding benchmark for event-driven risk assessment because prices aggregate dispersed beliefs in real time. Public text streams create a second information layer that price histories do not always summarize immediately. This paper examines whether AI-extracted public text improves calibrationsensitive downside-risk assessment beyond price-based benchmarks, and whether that value varies with the top-two price gap. The analysis uses Polymarket data covering 186 events and 22,071 event-day observations. It links an auditable daily text-measurement pipeline to rolling out-of-sample evaluation of next-day downside-tail risk. Nonlinear price-state modeling explains much of the improvement over a linear price-history baseline. AI-HGB adds a smaller text-layer increment beyond Price-HGB, with the clearest gains in calibration and selected threshold-based decision outcomes. State-contingency evidence shows that directional text becomes less diagnostic as the top-two price gap widens. The findings position AI-extracted text as an auditable measurement layer for risk-sensitive decision support.

title: When the Magazine Doesn't Empty: Cargill's Textualist Definition of Automatic Operation and the Federal-law Capture of Agentic Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: When the Magazine Doesn't Empty: Cargill's Textualist Definition of Automatic Operation and the Federal-law Capture of Agentic Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: In Garland v. Cargill, 602 U.S. 406 (2024), the Supreme Court resolved a long-running debate over the statutory definition of "machinegun" under the National Firearms Act of 1934 by holding that bump stocks do not satisfy the definition because each shot still requires a separate mechanical function of the trigger. The en banc Fifth Circuit in Cargill v. Garland, 57 F.4th 447 (5th Cir. 2023), reached the same conclusion through textualist statutory construction, and the Northern District of Texas extended the reasoning to forced reset triggers in National Association for Gun Rights v. Garland, 741 F. Supp. 3d 568 (N.D. Tex. 2024), with the Department of Justice subsequently dismissing the government's appeal and adopting the district court's position by settlement. Through this sequence the firearms-rights litigation movement secured a narrow, mechanical, textualist construction of "automatic" operation under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b): one input event producing continuous output, with no further input required between rounds. This Article argues that the textualist construction the firearms-rights movement won definitionally captures agentic artificial intelligence as it is now deployed. A single human deployment instruction directing an AI agent to execute multi-step tasks, manage resources, contract with third parties, and persist across time satisfies the literal textualist test that Cargill and NAGR established: a single function of the trigger producing continuous output without further input. The result is a cross-aisle doctrinal convergence that neither political coalition can easily resist. The textualist methodology that produced the firearms-rights victory binds the courts that apply it to other federal definitional questions. The functional-equivalence methodology that the gun-control movement urged in Cargill applies with greater force to agentic systems whose practical continuity exceeds anything contemplated in 1934. The 1934 statutory ceiling on autonomous operation, which caps at continuous fire until manual reload, leaves no doctrinal vocabulary for systems that source their own continuation through external compute markets, cryptocurrency wallets, and contracted services. This Article develops the statutory architecture, the post-Cargill application landscape, the application of the test to AI deployment, the doctrinal vacuum beyond the 1934 ceiling, the cross-aisle convergence, the standing implications, and the regulatory architecture that the federal regulatory state has used to address autonomous operation in adjacent contexts and that supplies a structural model for addressing it here. The honest political history of conditional anti-regulation, beginning with the Mulford Act of 1967 and the National Rifle Association's support for prohibiting open carry in response to the Black Panther Party, is addressed because it establishes the conditions under which contemporary anti-regulation coalitions support regulation in practice. Those conditions are present for agentic AI. The doctrinal road is built; both coalitions paved it; what remains is application.

title: Exchange Rate Channel of the Monetary Policy Transmission Mechanism: Evidence from West African Monetary Zone (WAMZ)
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Exchange Rate Channel of the Monetary Policy Transmission Mechanism: Evidence from West African Monetary Zone (WAMZ)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Personal

detail.abstract: This study examines the exchange rate channel of the monetary policy transmission mechanism in the West African Monetary Zone (WAMZ). The study is motivated by the persistent exchange-rate pressures, import dependence, inflation volatility and weak monetary policy transmission that continue to challenge macroeconomic stability and monetary integration in the zone. Using annual panel data for The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria and Sierra Leone from 1990 to 2025, the study employs a Panel Vector Error Correction Model following evidence of unit roots and cointegration among consumer price index, gross domestic product, exchange rate, monetary policy rate and money supply. Impulse response functions and forecast error variance decomposition are used to trace the dynamic effects of exchange-rate shocks on inflation and output. The findings show that the exchange rate channel is active in WAMZ, but its effect is stronger on inflation than on economic growth. Inflation responds positively and persistently to exchange-rate shocks, while output response is weaker and less stable. Variance decomposition further shows that exchange-rate shocks account for a rising share of inflation variation but explain only a modest share of output fluctuations. The study concludes that exchange-rate stability is central to inflation control and monetary policy credibility in WAMZ. It recommends stronger foreign exchange management, improved reserve buffers, better monetary-fiscal coordination and structural policies to reduce import dependence and strengthen domestic productive capacity.

title: A Review of Contest Theory: Equilibrium Strategies and Incentive Design
affiliations: Department of Economics, Nanjing University, Lingnan College, Sun Yat-sen University and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Review of Contest Theory: Equilibrium Strategies and Incentive Design
detail.abstract: Contest theory studies strategic competition among individuals or groups for rewards such as positions, market share, or rents. Owing to its wide applicability in settings such as rentseeking, promotion, litigation, political competition, and research and development (R&D), the theory has become a core field of microeconomics. Taking the classical models as our point of departure, this paper reviews the literature on equilibrium analysis and contest design. Within this scope, it examines several central issues, including prize allocation, contestant heterogeneity, budget constraints, contest technologies, and information disclosure. Finally, it summarizes promising directions for future theoretical research and potential extensions.

title: When Walls Become Targets: Strategic Speculation and Price Dynamics under Price Limit
affiliations: Peking University School of Economics and Peking University - School of Economics

detail.title: When Walls Become Targets: Strategic Speculation and Price Dynamics under Price Limit
detail.abstract: This study shows that price limit rules, though intended to stabilize markets, distort price dynamics by enabling strategic speculation. Through a rational expectations model, we demonstrate that price limits induce inherent post limit-up price-jumps by impeding full information incorporation. This motivates speculators to artificially push prices to the upper bound and profit at the expense of uninformed traders. The model predicts two distinct patterns: (1) stocks closing at upper price limits earn positive overnight returns followed by long-term reversals, and (2) stocks retreating from upper bound before market close incur significant loss for speculators and demonstrate a "collapse-underperformance" pattern. Empirical evidence confirms both predictions. China's 2020 GEM reform, which widened the price limit from 10% to 20%, provides further causal evidence that relaxed limits mitigate speculative distortions. Our model also captures several well-documented empirical patterns associated with price limits, including the magnet effect, volatility spillover, and delayed price discovery.

title: Exchange Rate Passthrough to Inflation: Evidence from Selected Sub-Saharan African Countries
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Exchange Rate Passthrough to Inflation: Evidence from Selected Sub-Saharan African Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Personal

detail.abstract: This study investigates the extent and dynamics of exchange rate pass-through (ERPT) to inflation in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana over the period 2010Q1-2025Q3 using a dynamic panel framework. Motivated by the open-economy New Keynesian Phillips Curve, inflation is modeled as a function of monetary policy stance, market interest rates, exchange rate movements, external trade performance, and aggregate output. The empirical analysis applies the Pooled Mean Group (PMG) estimator within a panel ARDL framework, which allows for country-specific short-run heterogeneity while imposing long-run equilibrium convergence. Panel unit root tests confirm a mixture of I(0) and I(1) processes, validating the ARDL-PMG approach. The results provide strong evidence of a stable long-run relationship between inflation and key macroeconomic fundamentals across the three economies. Short-run dynamics, however, are highly heterogeneous. In Nigeria, exchange rate depreciation exerts large and immediate inflationary effects, indicating rapid and substantial pass-through driven by high import dependence. In Kenya, inflation responds more strongly to monetary policy adjustments and output fluctuations, with muted short-run exchange rate effects. Ghana exhibits delayed but broader ERPT, with lagged exchange rate movements, monetary indicators, and real-sector conditions jointly shaping inflation dynamics. The error-correction terms are negative and significant across countries, indicating gradual adjustment toward long-run equilibrium, though at differing speeds. Overall, the findings demonstrate that ERPT in Sub-Saharan Africa is incomplete, asymmetric, and strongly country-specific in the short run, despite a shared long-run structure. The study underscores the need for coordinated inflation-management strategies that combine credible monetary policy, exchange rate stabilization, and structural reforms aimed at reducing import dependence and strengthening productive capacity.

title: Catalan Separatism: A Municipal Level Spatial Analysis of Population Density, Income, and Pro-Independence Sentiment

detail.title: Catalan Separatism: A Municipal Level Spatial Analysis of Population Density, Income, and Pro-Independence Sentiment
detail.abstract: This study tests the notion that Catalan separatism is driven by economic discontent and an urban–rural divide, examining whether pro‑independence sentiment is higher in rural areas facing greater economic challenges. Using municipal‑level data for 947 municipalities, it compares support for ERC and CDC in the 2016 parliamentary elections to population density and average household income, based on official Spanish administrative and survey data. Spatial statistics and regression techniques are applied to identify clustering and estimate the association between these factors and pro‑independence sentiment. The analysis reveals a clear urban–rural divide, with separatist support varying systematically across space, and shows that both population density and income are significantly related to independence preferences once spatial dependence is accounted for. Together, these patterns suggest that Catalan separatism cannot be reduced to simple economic grievance; the political leanings of neighboring municipalities exert a stronger influence on separatist support than average household income alone. More broadly, spatially embedded socioeconomic conditions play a central role in shaping political support for independence.

title: Active Mutual Fund Co-holdings and the Buy-side Peer Network
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU), City University of Hong Kong (CityU),  and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: Active Mutual Fund Co-holdings and the Buy-side Peer Network
detail.abstract: Peer groups in cross-stock return tests are usually specified by the researcher rather than observed from investor behavior. We use active mutual fund holdings to define peer groups from buy-side portfolio choices. In U.S. equities from 1990 to 2024, holdings-based peer returns predict next-month focal-stock returns. Predictability is concentrated among nearest holdings-space peers, absent for the least similar stocks, and robust to industry, shared-analyst, common-ownership, and characteristics-based controls. Peer fundamentals and earnings news also forecast focal-firm fundamentals. A value-weighted long-short portfolio earns 0.67% per month with significant alphas. Post-formation returns continue rather than reverse, and the signal is not subsumed by common ownership. The predictive slope is larger among high-friction focal stocks. A simple model links these patterns to limited investor coverage and gradual price adjustment.
