title: Organised Interests and the Neoliberal Turn: Assessing the Role of Organizations and Political Interests in Moving Mainstream Left Parties Toward Free Market Policies

detail.title: Organised Interests and the Neoliberal Turn: Assessing the Role of Organizations and Political Interests in Moving Mainstream Left Parties Toward Free Market Policies

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Foundation for Law & International Affairs Review, Volume 6, Issue 1, Pp. 149-174

detail.abstract: This paper examines why Western mainstream left parties embraced neoliberalism and free-market economic policies in the late 20th century. Existing literature often attributes this shift to the rising affluence of the median voter and the need for parties to adapt to changing economic conditions. While influential, this explanation is incomplete. Drawing on Hacker and Pierson's concept of "politics by organised interests", this paper argues that the neoliberal turn was primarily driven by changing relationships between mainstream left parties and their affiliated organizations and political constituencies. A historical single-case analysis of the American Democratic Party illustrates this dynamic. In the mid-20th century, the party relied heavily on labor unions and social justice groups, which wielded significant influence over its policy agenda, pushing it toward social democratic policies. From the 1970s onward, the declining electoral leverage of these groups reduced their influence, while the Democrats increasingly sought support from wealthy investors and business interests. This realignment pushed the party toward free-market economic policies that reflected the priorities of its new allies. These findings illuminate similar processes in other Western mainstream left parties and provide insight into their responses to the Great Recession and their electoral challenges in the 2010s. By foregrounding the role of organized interests, this paper offers a more robust explanation for the neoliberal drift of mainstream left parties than median-voter theories alone.

title: Causal Effects of Social Media Sentiment on Cryptocurrency Market Returns and Volatility
affiliations: , Westcliff University, Westcliff University and University of the Cumberlands

detail.title: Causal Effects of Social Media Sentiment on Cryptocurrency Market Returns and Volatility
detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets are highly sensitive to social media sentiment. Yet, the causal direction of these effects remains elusive owing to the predominance of correlational approaches that fail to address confounding and reverse causality. Against this backdrop, this study provides causally identified evidence on the impact of social media sentiment on cryptocurrency returns and volatility by applying a three-stage causal machine learning framework to a daily panel of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) over 159 trading days (January 2-June 12, 2023). The study utilized publicly available datasets of price data from CoinMarketCap and sentiment from the Crypto Twitter Influencer Sentiment Dataset. First, the Double Machine Learning Partially Linear Regression (DML-PLR) model removed high-dimensional observable confounding using crossfitted Random Forest nuisance estimators. Second, Partially Linear Instrumental Variables (PLIV) were used to correct for treatment endogeneity, confirmed in ETH importance-weighted sentiment via Hausman pre-testing. Third, Causal Forest was employed to estimate Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATEs) and assess heterogeneity across market regimes and influencer importance. Thereafter, a series of robustness checks (such as alternative nuisance learners, rolling-window stability analysis, leave-one-out tests, placebo and permutation diagnostics, lagged-treatment sensitivity, bootstrap and hyperparameter stability for Causal Forest, and macro-event confounder controls) were conducted to ascertain the reliability of the study findings. The results revealed a robust and consistently contrarian causal effect of sentiment on returns across all model specifications. The periods of elevated positive sentiment systematically precede price declines in tandem with a peak-optimism reversal mechanism. The strongest effect was observed for ETH, with a Causal Forest average treatment effect of-0.294 (p-value < 0.001). Significant heterogeneity was also identified. For BTC, the effect reversed sign across regimes, positive in bear markets (+0.161) and negative in bull markets (-0.133), while for ETH, the magnitude of the negative effect was amplified on high-influence days (p-value = 0.063). In contrast, no statistically significant causal effect of sentiment on realized volatility was detected, rejecting the uncertainty-amplification channel. The BTC contrarian effect remained stable across all diagnostics, whereas the ETH effect, though economically large, showed moderate sensitivity to temporal windows and heterogeneity specifications. Placebo and permutation tests rejected spurious correlation, and lagged-treatment results indicated that sentiment effects are primarily contemporaneous rather than persistent. Thus, the study advances the literature by providing rigorously causal evidence on the crypto-sentiment nexus, moving beyond the limitations of prior correlational analyses.

title: Buy It Now Or Later? An Experimental Study of Second-price Auction with Buy Price
affiliations: Daito Bunka University - Department of Economics, Future University Hakodate and Daito Bunka University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Buy It Now Or Later? An Experimental Study of Second-price Auction with Buy Price
detail.abstract: This paper experimentally investigates bidder behavior in second-price auctions with a buyout option. We focus on how competition among bidders, time preference, and ambiguity about both factors affect the decision to exercise the buyout option. Using a laboratory experiment, we vary the number of bidders and introduce a rate of decay in bidder's valuation that captures the speed of loss of their interest to the object for sale. We also incorporate Knightian uncertainty regarding these factors to examine how ambiguity influences behavior. In addition, we compare the explanatory power of the standard rational model and the Level-k model. The results show that both competition and time preference significantly affect buyout decisions, consistent with theoretical predictions. In contrast, the effects of ambiguity are mixed: participants do not behave as the maximin expected utility model predicts, and their choices differ across parameters. Furthermore, buyout behavior is better explained by the Level-k model than by the standard rational model, indicating systematic deviations from optimal decision-making.

title: Outsourcing Extinction: Economic Complexity and the Geography of Biodiversity Loss
affiliations: University of Northern British Columbia, International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and World Bank Group

detail.title: Outsourcing Extinction: Economic Complexity and the Geography of Biodiversity Loss
detail.abstract: Does the structure of an economy, beyond its level of income, shape biodiversity loss? We relate the Red List Index of aggregate species extinction risk to economic complexity for up to 179 countries between 1993 and 2019. Conditional on income per capita, greater economic complexity raises extinction risk within countries: a one-standard-deviation increase in the Economic Complexity Index lowers the Red List Index by about one to two percent. The result is robust to country and period fixed effects, a long-difference specification, sectoral controls, and instrumental-variables estimation using product-space diversification potential. The mechanism is not domestic. Agricultural land use, forest cover, input intensity, and agricultural productivity do not mediate the relationship, nor are they systematically affected by economic complexity. Instead, complex economies displace biodiversity pressure abroad. In a bilateral matrix of extinction-risk footprints, they are net importers of biodiversity loss, sourcing an increasing share of their footprint from other countries' species. Imports from biome-sharing regions predict subsequent declines in domestic extinction-risk indices, evidence for a range-overlap channel linking foreign habitat conversion to home-country biodiversity outcomes. Economic complexity therefore reorganizes the geography of extinction risk rather than reducing it. Structural transformation does not, on its own, deliver decoupling from biodiversity loss, and conservation policies based on territorial indicators understate the biodiversity cost of complex economies.

title: Crisis, Compassion, and Capital: The Economics of Global Charitable Giving

detail.title: Crisis, Compassion, and Capital: The Economics of Global Charitable Giving
detail.abstract: Do major crises create new charitable capital, or do they primarily reallocate donor attention? We study this question using the universe of nearly 50,000 projects across 201 countries on GlobalGiving between 2003 and 2025. Exploiting the Russo-Ukrainian war as an exogenous shock to global humanitarian attention, we show that funding to Ukraine-related projects increased dramatically following the war, while funding to non-Ukraine projects declined. The response operates primarily through donor participation rather than donation size, indicating that crises reshape who gives as much as they reshape how much people give. The evidence further suggests that crises generate both new charitable resources and crowd-out of less salient causes, rather than representing either pure additionality or pure substitution. We also develop and test a framework showing that crises reshape charitable giving through both donor preference shifts and narrative competition. The dominant effect is a broad shift toward disaster-response and identifiable-beneficiary appeals, while crowding-out is concentrated in a limited set of narrative frames heavily associated with the crisis. Finally, we document substantial geographic disparities in charitable funding and show that crisis-driven attention amplifies these inequalities, widening funding gaps across regions. Taken together, our findings suggest that charitable giving operates in an attention-constrained market where major crises reshape both the level and distribution of philanthropic capital.

title: Risk and Illiquidity Premia in the Cross Section of OTC Assets
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and

detail.title: Risk and Illiquidity Premia in the Cross Section of OTC Assets

declarations.funderStatement: Semih Uslu acknowledges the General Research Support Fund Award from the Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic model of a multi-asset over-the-counter (OTC) market that operates via search and bargaining, and test its implications for illiquidity premia and market liquidity in the cross section of assets. Investors can trade each asset bilaterally subject to search frictions or trade an entire portfolio with specialized dealers by paying a fixed cost. General-equilibrium effects shape the cross section of liquidity and asset returns: assets with higher exposure to search frictions have higher return premia, lower trade volume, and higher price dispersion, and alleviating the search frictions in one asset can affect different empirical measures of other assets' liquidity in opposite directions. Using transaction-level data from the US corporate bond market and proxying for the inverse of search frictions with dealer centrality, we find substantial empirical support for our theory's implications, including its cross-asset mechanism.

title: The Euro Area Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto and Independent

detail.title: The Euro Area Bank Lending Channel of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: The bank lending channel is a cornerstone of monetary policy transmission in the Euro area, where bank credit constitutes the primary source of external finance for firms and households. This paper examines the transmission of monetary policy through this channel using a medium-scale Bayesian Structural Vector Autoregression (BSVAR) model estimated over 2006Q1-2024Q2, identified via sign restrictions normalised to a 25-basis-point contractionary shock. Robustness is assessed via a large Factor-Augmented VAR (FAVAR) model and local projections using the Jarociński and Karadi (2020) high-frequency monetary policy (MP) and central bank information (CBI) shock series. The results confirm the presence of the bank lending channel: a contractionary monetary policy shock contracts real activity and inflation, raises bank loan rates, increases financial volatility, and tightens credit conditions, with effects peaking within four to six quarters. The MP shock accounts for approximately 6-8 percent of the forecast error variance of output and loan rates at medium-term horizons. The CBI shock produces distinctly weaker real effects, underscoring the empirical importance of separating pure rate decisions from central bank signaling.

title: Subjective Risk Premia in Bond and FX Markets
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London - School of Economics and Finance and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: Subjective Risk Premia in Bond and FX Markets
detail.abstract: Using a thirty-year monthly panel of professional forecasts across ten countries, we measure subjective bond and currency risk premia. Subjective bond premia are on average negative; currency premia follow the carry-trade ordering; and yield forecast errors are systematically negative while exchange rate errors are unbiased. Subjective bond premia vary counter-cyclically with expected growth, while subjective currency premia are explained by foreign growth expectations, but only in the cross section. An international habit-formation model rationalizes these patterns: a moderate positive distortion in beliefs about consumption growth drives subjective risk premia across international markets through the surplus-consumption channel.

title: Women's Commuting After Childbirth: Evidence from U.S. Panel Data
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Women's Commuting After Childbirth: Evidence from U.S. Panel Data
detail.abstract: Post-childbirth commute burden is a potential source for disparity in labor market experience and earnings between men and women. A recent notable example is \cite{Bütikofer2025}, who document that the commuting patterns of Norwegian parents diverge substantially and persistently after their first childbirth, with mothers reducing commuting distance by 19 kilometers compared to 10 kilometers for fathers. We extend this line of inquiry using U.S. data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics that cover two distinct periods: 1970--1986 and 2011--2019. We find patterns that differ in important ways from the Norwegian experience. While U.S. mothers exit the labor force at substantially higher rates than fathers following childbirth, mothers who remain employed show little change in commuting time or distance relative to their pre-birth patterns or to fathers---a robust finding across four decades and across both time and distance measures of commute. These contrasting patterns call for more cross-country research on post-childbirth commute changes in both time and distance.

title: Central Bank Communication Graphs for Bank of England and Federal Reserve Documents, 1998-2026
affiliations: Middle East Technical University

detail.title: Central Bank Communication Graphs for Bank of England and Federal Reserve Documents, 1998-2026
detail.abstract: This Data Descriptor presents a temporal semantic graph dataset derived from public Bank of England and Federal Reserve communications released between 1998 and 2026. The dataset represents 2,872 valid documents as graph snapshots in the Monetary Communication Graph for mat, with 2,872 document container nodes, 24,010 semantic nodes, and 24,185 typed semantic edges. Unlike flat-text corpora, the format separates recurring policy-relevant communication channels, cited evidence, document-grounded inference, market-relevance fields, and within document semantic relations. The release includes model-ready document, node, and edge tables; 51,067 text embeddings; fixed semantic slot mappings for temporal modelling; schema definitions; prompts; validation outputs; helper scripts; figures; and file manifests with check sums. The dataset supports reusable research on central-bank communication, monetary-policy discourse, market-expectation formation, temporal semantic graphs, representation learning, and dynamic graph modelling.

title: Memorized but Not Realized: Frontier Language Models Precisely Recall Financial Fundamentals, but It Does Not Become Trading Skill
affiliations: University of Geneva

detail.title: Memorized but Not Realized: Frontier Language Models Precisely Recall Financial Fundamentals, but It Does Not Become Trading Skill

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, their data, or animal subjects. It uses firm-level financial-market data and publicly released language models only; ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no competing interests. The research was conducted independently; it was not funded by, and does not rely on the proprietary data or systems of, any commercial trading entity.

detail.abstract: LLM "AI-trading" benchmarks are routinely scored by replaying historical markets, raising a contamination concern: a model that has memorized an asset's realized outcome cannot generate honest out-of-sample skill, so backtest performance may be recall rather than foresight. We build a white-box-to-black-box validated leakage instrument and use it to ask the decision-relevant question prior work leaves open: does memorization capacity actually transmit to trading decisions? We report a dissociation. Capacity is large, precise, and universal: across 16 open models (10 vendors) and three commercial APIs, models prefer the realized revenue over magnitude-matched (±15%) counterfactuals at 0.23–0.81 (chance 0.20) and freely generate the figure within 10% for up to 89% of famous firm-years, while no-leak chronologically-consistent baselines sit at chance. Recall is cutoff-bounded: exploiting the models' different training cutoffs, it collapses to chance for facts dated after a model's cutoff (within-model t = −6.6, 18 of 19 models), the design-based signature of memorization rather than estimation. Applied to the realized return itself — the variable a backtest fears — recall is at chance with no cutoff signature: these models memorize fundamentals, not prices. Realization, by contrast, is null across five independent tests, including a cross-sectional ranking task (N ≈ 5,700 per model) and a realistic StockBench-style backtest over six open and frontier-API agents; an apparent agentic signal (+9.9pp, t = 4.07) is shown to be a firm-prominence confound that vanishes under firm fixed effects (β = −0.018). A pre-registered, dependence-corrected power analysis bounds any residual post-cutoff skill: on a ≈2,000-name post-cutoff universe the minimum detectable mean |IC| is ≈0.012–0.016, below the 0.02–0.05 band where real cross-sectional strategies operate. The contribution is a validated leakage instrument, an identification result showing why memorization is invisible to any pre-cutoff backtest, and the finding that, for the signals we test, LLM memorization of the market does not become measurable market skill.

title: News Duration Risk and Asset Prices

detail.title: News Duration Risk and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: This paper studies asset pricing when investors observe the size and frequency of aggregate shocks but disagree about their duration. Motivated by survey evidence that professional forecasters differ in the speed at which they expect output shocks to dissipate, I develop a continuous-time endowment economy in which agents agree on the probabilities and magnitudes of transitory news shocks but hold different priors over their decay rate. A shock therefore starts a learning episode: its impact is observed immediately, while its persistence is revealed only through the subsequent recovery path. The equilibrium separates size and probability risks from news-duration risk. Risk sharing is likelihood-weighted, and the stochastic discount factor depends on both aggregate marginal utility and the consumption-weighted distribution of beliefs. Duration learning reallocates consumption and wealth, changes the beliefs of the marginal investor, and moves discount rates, risk premia, and hedging demands. In a three-decay-rate implementation, persistent-duration evidence raises the relevance of future cash-flow consequences and strengthens predictability, whereas evidence of rapid dissipation compresses compensation by shortening the expected life of the shock. These effects appear in valuation ratios, derivative positions, and bond and equity yields. The analysis shows that news-duration risk is a distinct asset-pricing force: even when investors agree on what happened, disagreement about how long it will matter is priced.

title: Ownership Structure and Bank Stability: Evidence from the 2023 Banking Crisis
affiliations: University of North Texas and University of Georgia - Department of Finance

detail.title: Ownership Structure and Bank Stability: Evidence from the 2023 Banking Crisis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We examine how the composition of institutional and insider ownership relates to bank vulnerability during the March 2023 banking crisis. Using 463 publicly traded U.S. banks, we find that higher aggregate institutional ownership is associated with worse crisis-period returns, but that this relation masks heterogeneity across investor types. Hedge fund ownership is associated with exposure to higherrisk bank characteristics, consistent with risk selection, and this relation survives across subsamples and specifications. Investment advisor ownership predicts larger short-term declines, consistent with pricepressure dynamics, although this relation is weaker and is supported primarily in the full cross-section rather than in a narrower subsample of larger banks for which more detailed data are available. We find no evidence of pre-crisis insider or institutional exit from banks that subsequently experienced the largest crisis-period declines, alleviating the concern that ownership at the onset of the crisis reflects anticipatory portfolio choices by informed investors. This inference is stronger for insiders than for institutions, since quarterly 13F filings limit our ability to observe late-window institutional trading. Moreover, insider ownership attenuates the negative hedge fund-return relation, consistent with managerial equity stakes dampening the risk-taking pressures associated with hedge fund ownership. These associations are not absorbed by observable proxies for uninsured-deposit exposure and unrealized securities losses. Overall, institutional ownership composition contains information about crisis-period bank performance that the aggregate level alone does not reveal.

title: Fixed Deep Residual Networks with Multi-Objective Proximal Policy Optimization for Adaptive Trading

detail.title: Fixed Deep Residual Networks with Multi-Objective Proximal Policy Optimization for Adaptive Trading
detail.abstract: Financial markets are highly noisy and unpredictable. Trading strategies are required to simultaneously account for short-term price fluctuations and long-term structural regimes. Furthermore, developing a quantitative system that balances multiple conflicting objectives, such as maximizing profit while minimizing downside risk, according to shifting preferences remains a significant challenge. To address these limitations, we propose an adaptive trading framework that integrates a Deep Residual Network (DRN) with a single multi-objective Reinforcement Learning (RL) model. Operating over raw technical indicators, our DRN architecture utilizes residual skip connections to impose a structured, nonlinear geometric transformation on the raw technical indicator matrix, producing stable 32-dimensional latent embeddings that are held fixed throughout the reinforcement learning optimization phase. Rather than training a computationally heavy concatenation of multiple discrete RL networks, our system trains a single unified agent directly on dynamic objective sets to learn the continuous relationship between different preference combinations and the fixed DRN market representations. Experimental results demonstrate that this pipeline delivers steadier, more robust trading performance along the Pareto-optimal frontier, offering a highly scalable and adaptive alternative to traditional multi-network systems.

title: Going Local: Decentralization, Bureaucratic Capacity and Public Spending Efficiency
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome - Department of Social Sciences and Economics and

detail.title: Going Local: Decentralization, Bureaucratic Capacity and Public Spending Efficiency
detail.abstract: Decentralization reforms are typically justified on efficiency grounds, yet their distributional consequences remain poorly understood. We show that a uniform administrative decentralization reform can generate aggregate efficiency gains while simultaneously widening territorial disparities, depending on the pre-existing bureaucratic capacity of local governments. Exploiting spatial variation in the implementation of a major Italian constitutional reform of 2001 through a matched difference-indifferences design and data covering 1998-2007, we document significant average efficiency gains. However, aggregate gains mask a distributional divide: highcapacity municipalities achieve efficiency improvements through cost optimization, maintaining their pre-reform growth trajectory, while low-capacity municipalities concentrate efforts on visible short-term gains and experience an average income loss of approximately 116 per capita. We identify four mechanisms driving this divergence: enhanced fiscal accountability through greater reliance on local taxation, a strategic shift toward income taxation paired with greater leniency in tax collection among low-capacity municipalities, incumbents' re-election incentives, and local governments' responsiveness to citizens' expressed preferences for decentralization. This study provides important policy implications for understanding distributional consequences of decentralization processes and inform their optimal design.

title: Data Transport, AI, and Growth
affiliations: University of South Carolina, Stanford University - Hoover Institution and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Data Transport, AI, and Growth
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence services require model-building and computation (model/compute) together with data transport, the technical and legal work that makes usable data available to computing, storage, monitoring, and learning systems. We develop an endogenous-growth model in which firms invest in both. Because data are nonrival, data-transport barriers create a double wedge: they raise current delivery costs and reduce data available for future innovation. Model/compute innovation alone generally cannot sustain growth when data-delivery costs remain incompressible; data-transport innovation restores balanced growth. Regulations that fragment data use across agencies or jurisdictions reduce growth, while trust-enhancing safeguards can raise it.

title: Randomized Neural Networks for estimation of exposure profiles and Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) for American Equity Options
affiliations: University of Warsaw,  and University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences

detail.title: Randomized Neural Networks for estimation of exposure profiles and Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) for American Equity Options
detail.abstract: This thesis studies the use of randomized neural networks for the estimation of exposure profiles and unilateral CVA of American options within a Monte Carlo framework. The analysis is carried out separately under both Black-Scholes and Heston dynamics, combining American option valuation, expected exposure and potential future exposure estimation, and unilateral CVA calculation with portfolio netting effects. The numerical experiment compares this approach with the classical Least-Squares Monte Carlo (LSM) used as a benchmark in both low-dimensional single-asset and high-dimensional multiasset scenarios, and also includes a path convergence test and a sensitivity analysis. The results show that the randomized feedforward neural network approach preserves convergence to the LSM benchmark when it is extended from pricing to exposure and CVA estimation, while its main advantage appears in high-dimensional problems, where it scales more efficiently and leads to lower computational cost. These results support the use of randomized neural networks as a useful alternative for exposure and CVA estimation in high-dimensional American-style options.

title: The Heterogeneous Impact of the Energy Transition
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto,  and University College Cork

detail.title: The Heterogeneous Impact of the Energy Transition

declarations.funderStatement: Matteo Bondesan acknowledges financial support under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.1, Call for tender No. 1409 published on 14.9.2022 by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR), funded by the European Union – NextGenerationEU– Project Title ”Measuring, managing and hedging indirect climate-transition risks” – CUP P20228CHNL - Grant Assignment Decree No. 1376 adopted on 01/09/2023 by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR).

detail.abstract: The energy transition is inflationary in the short run and deflationary in the long run, with uneven intergenerational effects. We develop a climate OLG model extending Diamond (1965) to a dual-sector economy with a brown fossil-fuel sector and a green renewable sector. A carbon tax shifts capital and labour toward the more capital-intensive green sector, while a convex damage function maps accumulated atmospheric carbon into output losses and raises the optimal Pigouvian tax over time. The transition is inflationary at first because the tax passes through into brown-sector prices, but becomes deflationary in the long run as learning-by-doing boosts green productivity. The tax burdens older cohorts through lower savings returns, whereas younger cohorts face lower wages but benefit from reduced future climate damages. A revenue-neutral transfer that directs more than half of revenues to the elderly cohort equalises welfare impacts. We derive a Green Golden Rule showing that efficient climate policy requires carbon taxation combined with intergenerational transfers.

detail.abstract:
Current artificial memory systems store knowledge as points in Euclidean space, destroying
hierarchical relationships and suffering from catastrophic forgetting under concept drift. While
static hyperbolic embeddings offer improved capacity for tree-structured data, they remain rigid
against structural evolution. We present the Poincaré Cortex, a hyperbolic cognitive memory
substrate that continuously adapts its local curvature via Ricci flow. By replacing computationally
expensive Ollivier–Ricci curvature with effective resistance curvature (ERC), we achieve real-
time updates in $O(|E_k| \log |V_k|)$ per insertion, where $E_k, V_k$ are edges and nodes in a
$k$-hop neighbourhood. We prove two results: (1) discrete Ricci flow converges to a stationary
configuration with bounded curvature variance (Theorem 1); and (2) under classical thermodynamic
assumptions, the energy cost of curvature adaptation is bounded by the agent's PCES score
(Theorem 2). Vitality—a measure of node usage—modulates curvature evolution: high-vitality
regions flatten for rapid access, while dormant nodes sink to the Dark Matter reservoir, a formal
archival region with resurrection via geodesic search. During offline consolidation cycles (the
Dream Cycle, analogous to sleep), the system runs Ricci flow without new data, synthesizing ghost
nodes via geodesic interpolation to minimize global free energy. Crucially, monitoring curvature
variance provides a geometric early-warning signal for cognitive drift and adversarial attacks,
triggering safety interrupts before performance degrades. The Poincaré Cortex is the geometric
substrate for the Tharine Theorem (NSP-01): the fidelity term $F_i = \exp(-\lambda d_H^2)$ is
computed from hyperbolic distance, and high curvature variance serves as a geometric proxy for
elevated variational surprise.
This is NSP-02 in the 17-paper Nexus Sovereign Physics & AGI research program, establishing the
geometric memory substrate for the Tharine Theorem (NSP-01).

title: Breaking the Silence on the Hidden Reality of Male Victims in Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study from Pangasinan, Philippines
affiliations: Pangasinan State University

detail.title: Breaking the Silence on the Hidden Reality of Male Victims in Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study from Pangasinan, Philippines
detail.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) against men remains an underexplored public health concern shaped by gender normativity, cultural context, and structural inequality. In the Philippines, patriarchal social organization and the explicit exclusion of male victims from primary domestic violence legislation have compounded their marginalization in research and policy. Guided by the Ecological Model of Violence, Hegemonic Masculinity Theory, and the IPV Stigma Model, this study examined the prevalence, forms, and contextual dynamics of IPV among heterosexual men in a selected municipality in Pangasinan, Philippines. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed, involving 21 purposively selected male respondents who self-reported IPV victimization. Quantitative data were gathered through a researcher-developed questionnaire assessing emotional, physical, sexual, financial, and technological abuse using five-point Likert items; qualitative responses were analyzed through Braun and Clarke’s (2006) six-phase thematic analysis. Emotional abuse was most prevalent (M = 2.743), whereas physical abuse was least (M = 1.524). Withholding intimacy as punishment was disproportionately common within the sexual abuse typology (M = 3.571), and financial control was the most frequent financial abuse indicator (M = 3.619). Formal disclosure rates were critically low: 19.0% reported to authorities and 14.3% sought professional help. Exploratory Chi-square analyses identified significant associations between educational attainment and technological abuse (p = .043), monthly income and sexual abuse (p = .039), and relationship duration and financial abuse (p = .037). Thematic analysis yielded four themes: stigma of male victimhood; community as judge; emotional entrapment; and the absence of gendered legal protection. Findings underscore the need for gender-inclusive legislative reform, culturally responsive support services, and expanded regional research on male IPV victimization.

title: Advanced AI and Civilizational Disruption Risk: A Public-source Scenario Analysis of Critical Infrastructure, Strategic Stability, and Recovery Pathways

detail.abstract: This working paper asks what an advanced artificial intelligence system, or a person directing one, could and could not realistically do to destabilize global civilization, and bounds the answer using public sources only. It separates pathways that are physically and operationally supported from those that are not. Three widely repeated claims are shown to lack support: that an AI system could transmit through the electrical grid, that it could permanently brick electronics on a universal scale, and that it could launch nuclear weapons absent the access, authority, and physical safeguards that doctrine and engineering impose. The supported risks are different in kind. They are concentrated, mostly recoverable disruptions that propagate through shared software, cloud, and information-technology dependencies; large-scale information disorder and automated fraud; financial-market volatility amplified by automation and false information; and localized operational-technology disruption where remote access and weak segmentation exist. The paper applies a sixteen-sector critical-infrastructure assessment, a conditional Day 1 to Year 1 scenario framework, and recovery and defensive-measures analysis mapped to existing federal frameworks, including the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Every load-bearing claim is labeled by its level of support and confidence, and all seventy-seven evidentiary sources are individually verified against primary records, and the author's related work is cited separately and not counted among them. The central finding is that the realistic threat is serious but not civilization-ending: it strains systems that depend on continuous, trusted operation, and it is best met by disciplined implementation of existing resilience and governance practice rather than by novel countermeasures.

title: Policy, Technology, and Economic Efficiency of Infrastructure Energy Investment: A Strategic Analysis for a Low-carbon Future
affiliations: Qingdao Binhai University, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law,  and Qingdao Binhai University

detail.title: Policy, Technology, and Economic Efficiency of Infrastructure Energy Investment: A Strategic Analysis for a Low-carbon Future
detail.abstract:
This study provides a comprehensive strategic analysis of infrastructure energy
investment in the context of the global low-carbon transition. Integrating quanti-
tative panel data analysis across 15 countries (2010–2023), detailed case studies of
Germany, the United States, China, and the European Union, and scenario sim-
ulations through 2050, we examine how policy, technology, and economic factors
interact to determine investment effectiveness. Using panel data from 15 countries
over the period 2010–2023, we find that renewable energy investment is system-
atically associated with higher economic growth and lower carbon emissions after
controlling for country and year fixed effects. Because investment enters the re-
gression in logarithms, effect sizes should be interpreted as semi-elasticities. A 10%
increase in renewable investment (i.e., ∆ ln Investment ≈ ln(1.10)) is associated
with about 0.027 percentage points higher GDP growth (0.285 × ln(1.10)). For interpretability, a doubling of investment (∆ ln Investment = ln 2) corresponds to
about 0.198 percentage points higher GDP growth (0.285 × ln 2), holding other
factors constant.Among policy instruments, carbon pricing exerts the strongest
influence on investment returns, with a sensitivity index of 0.78, underscoring the
central role of policy credibility in shaping infrastructure investment outcomes. The
ablation study demonstrates that the full integrated policy-technology framework
achieves 92.5% policy effectiveness compared to 45.2% for carbon pricing alone,
highlighting the importance of comprehensive approaches. Scenario simulations
indicate that ambitious policy action can achieve 92.5% renewable energy share
and reduce emissions to 8.2 Gt by 2050, while generating 72.8 million clean energy
jobs. We propose an integrated investment framework that offers actionable guid-
ance for policymakers designing carbon pricing and green finance mechanisms, and
for investors optimizing risk-adjusted returns in clean energy portfolios. This re-
search contributes to the literature by providing empirically grounded insights into
the conditions under which infrastructure energy investment can simultaneously
advance economic growth and environmental sustainability objectives.

title: Leveraging AI to Identify Small Business Regulations at the Federal, State, and Local Levels
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution and Salisbury University

detail.title: Leveraging AI to Identify Small Business Regulations at the Federal, State, and Local Levels
detail.abstract: We introduce a novel database of small business exemptions at the 3-digit NAICS industry level for 48 US States in 2023. Our dataset is derived using Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is validated using more traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods. We demonstrate that this data is correlated with other measures of small business friendliness at the state level. Furthermore, we apply our LLM classifier to the US Code of Federal Regulations and show that the industry pattern of small business regulation at the state level is similar to industry patterns at the federal level. We find that industries with higher levels of small business exemptions exhibit greater economic dynamism (i.e., more establishment and job formation). Finally, we extend the same LLM-based screening approach to municipal ordinances, analyzing 3,241 jurisdictions. This municipal extension shows that local "small business" definitions are substantially more heterogeneous than those used at the state and federal levels, varying widely across jurisdictions and policy domains.

title: On Volatility-managed Portfolios: The Role of Conditional Factor Correlations
affiliations: CATÓLICA-LISBON School of Business & Economics, Hanken School of Economics - Department of Finance and Statistics and

detail.title: On Volatility-managed Portfolios: The Role of Conditional Factor Correlations

declarations.funderStatement: Pedro Barroso acknowledges the support from FCT – Portuguese Foundation of Science and Technology for the project “UID/GES/00407/2020.

detail.abstract: Out of the nine volatility-managed equity factors employed by Moreira and Muir (2017), only three (momentum, ROE, and betting-against-beta) produce robust significantly positive alphas over the 1967-2024 period. However, the evidence for portfolios of factors is considerably stronger. Concretely, the scaled mean-variance-efficient combination of the five factors of Fama and French (2015) produces significantly positive alphas, even when imposing no leverage. The explanation for these apparent contradictory results lies on the important role played by conditional correlations among the individual factors. Our results suggest that the profitability of volatility-management is best judged when incorporating the diversification benefits associated with factors.

title: Equilibrium Analysis for Strategic Information Revelation in Data Markets

detail.title: Equilibrium Analysis for Strategic Information Revelation in Data Markets
detail.abstract: The accelerating demand for high-quality training data by large language model developers has intensified the need for principled mechanisms to trade datasets under asymmetric information. We propose a tractable signaling framework in which sellers choose the fraction of a dataset to disclose and buyers update beliefs via Bayesian inference; crucially, disclosure imposes implicit costs through diminishing marginal data quality, which differentially constrains low-quality sellers. We derive analytical conditions for the existence of pooling and separating equilibria, characterize how equilibrium disclosure policies depend on the distribution of seller types and buyer priors, and identify parameter regimes in which markets are most vulnerable to adverse selection. Complementing closed-form results, numerical simulations illustrate how strategic information revelation functions as a credible quality signal and alters bidding and allocation outcomes. Our findings yield actionable implications for the design of data-market institutions (e.g., standardized disclosure, certification, and audit mechanisms) and contribute to the theory of information economics and mechanism design by offering a unified framework to analyze and regulate emerging data marketplaces.

title: Gradient-Based Structural Optimization of Offshore Jackets via Differentiable Physics Simulations
affiliations: Tianjin University and Tianjin University

detail.title: Gradient-Based Structural Optimization of Offshore Jackets via Differentiable Physics Simulations
detail.abstract: Gradient-based structural optimization is attractive for offshore jacket design, but is often demonstrated with simplified loading and surrogate performance measures. In practice, jackets are designed under nonlinear, geometry-dependent wave-current loading and assessed using code-oriented criteria such as unity checks (UC). This paper presents an end-to-end differentiable analysis-and-optimization workflow for deepwater offshore jackets, implemented in JAX. The framework combines (i) a differentiable 3D beam finite element model, (ii) realistic, designdependent hydrodynamic loading based on fifth-order Stokes wave kinematics, a power-law current profile, and Morison drag/inertia forces, and (iii) UC-based structural integrity assessment for an ultimate limit state sea state. Leveraging JAX just-in-time compilation and reverse-mode automatic differentiation, we formulate two complementary gradient-based design problems: a topology optimization by screening member groups using compliance gradients, and a shape optimization that adjusts level elevations and plan dimensions to homogenize UC utilization. Verification against the OC4 reference jacket confirms the fidelity of the differentiable FEM model, and the optimization studies illustrate how the proposed pipeline can identify structurally important members, prune low-sensitivity braces, and tune global geometry, offering a computationally efficient alternative to gradient-free metaheuristics for realistic offshore jacket design.

title: The Overdetermination of African Conflict and the Strategic Defeat of Interventionism in Mogadishu, 1993

detail.title: The Overdetermination of African Conflict and the Strategic Defeat of Interventionism in Mogadishu, 1993
detail.abstract: African armed conflict is a historical-institutional anomaly, not an essential property of the continent, and what any external intervention can hope to achieve depends on that distinction. Africa leads in the number of active state-based conflicts and in a disproportionate share of violence directed against civilians without thereby concentrating the majority of annual battle deaths: the weight shifts with the metric chosen. The U.S. operation of 3 October 1993 in Mogadishu failed not through tactical inferiority but through a design error-a small force with large political objectives committed to a city it did not territorially control. The reconstruction of the episode is governed by a documentary asymmetry that renders any clean count of Somali casualties untenable and forces the statute of testimony apart from the statute of the record. The institutional argument fails if used to predict individual conduct or to dissolve the exceptions, beginning with Mauritius, the only African country with no involvement in conflict for six consecutive years.

detail.abstract: The Self-Evolution Problem — the risk that a cognitively capable agent will modify its own objective function, safety invariants, or identity — constitutes the most fundamental open challenge in aligned artificial intelligence. This paper introduces the Constitutional Manifold framework: a formally constrained safety envelope, grounded in geometry and thermodynamics, that specifies which self-modifications are constitutionally admissible for the NEXUS Sovereign cognitive organism. We make four independently verifiable contributions. First (Theorems 1-2), we prove that the Constitutional Manifold is invariant under the projection operator, and that Port-Hamiltonian dissipation bounds mutation energy — preventing the agent from generating net internal energy to violate its Markov blanket. Second (Theorems 3-4), we derive that Ricci curvature variance in the Poincaré Cortex provides a formally grounded early-warning signal for constitutional drift (3.2x detection speedup, p < 0.001), and that Koopman spectral analysis enables predictive safety checks in O(n^2) time before any mutation executes. The complete system — the 13-layer InvariantShield — achieved 100% adversarial mutation block rate across 10,000 simulation trials and 98.4% fallback switching success. title: Nuclear Geoeconomics: A Trilateral Action Plan for South Korea, Japan, and the US
affiliations: and Rice University

detail.title: Nuclear Geoeconomics: A Trilateral Action Plan for South Korea, Japan, and the US
detail.abstract: This paper argues that nuclear power is re-emerging as a decisive geoeconomic instrument in an AI-driven era where electricity abundance confers national security and industrial advantage. China and Russia are moving fastest, pairing standardized reactor designs with state-backed finance and long-term fuel-service relationships that can shape geopolitical alignment for decades. HENRY HAGGARD AND GABRIEL COLLINS1 The United States, South Korea, and Japan can compete by integrating their strengths—US capital and innovation, Korea’s proven delivery and heavy-industry foundry capacity, and Japanese precision manufacturing—into a joint design-build-finance platform for domestic deployment and exports. Because capital dominates nuclear levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), the plan prioritizes export credit and bundled data center– nuclear plant packages, while managing Korea’s fiscal exposure.

title: The United States and Canada: Twin Crises of Governance
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: The United States and Canada: Twin Crises of Governance
detail.abstract: The United States is suffering a crisis of governance, and therefore Canada is in crisis as well. The current American "crisis of democracy" is one of several experienced since 1900, all triggered by a collapse in confidence about national strategy in domestic and foreign affairs. The current crisis began before Trump's election in 2016: since then, Trump's actions have intensified and mutated the crisis. His policies since 2025 have also up-ended Canadian politics, triggering reconsideration of national strategy in that country too. The United States and Canada are both liberal democratic federations. But there are institutional and cultural differences between the countries that affect the pace and depth of strategic realignment. This chapter reminds us why the field of public administration must pay more attention to macro-level questions about system design, and think more explicitly about the preservation of democratic values, than it has in recent decades.

title: Cryptic Connections: Uncovering News-implied Linkages Between Banks and Digital Asset Service Providers
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Quantitative Supervision & Research, University of Connecticut, Quantitative Supervision and Research - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond and Federal Reserve Banks - Quantitative Supervision & Research

detail.title: Cryptic Connections: Uncovering News-implied Linkages Between Banks and Digital Asset Service Providers
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates how financial news can be used to reveal otherwise obscure links between banks in the U.S. financial sector and private companies, with a particular emphasis on emerging financial activities. Although the existing literature largely relies on stock return-based networks to analyze interconnectedness, such approaches are limited to publicly traded firms and can miss key network participants. We propose a novel method that leverages co-mentions in financial news articles to map connections between major banks and private digital asset service providers (DASPs). After mapping bank-DASP connections, we explore shock transmission across the network using the collapse of FTX as a case study. While our methodology is broadly applicable, a critical contribution of our approach is that it allows us to understand the nature of novel activities as banks' roles are evolving and regulatory frameworks remain in flux. Despite its simplicity, our approach highlights the value of news-based network analysis in identifying relationships in markets where key participants are privately held and thus absent from traditional market-based datasets.

title: Rate Sensitivity and Employment: A Shift-Share Difference-in-Differences Analysis of Federal Funds Rate Changes on County-Level Employment
affiliations: DePaul University

detail.title: Rate Sensitivity and Employment: A Shift-Share Difference-in-Differences Analysis of Federal Funds Rate Changes on County-Level Employment
detail.abstract: This paper estimates the heterogeneous employment effects of federal funds rate changes across U.S. counties using a shift-share difference-in-differences design. Exploiting variation in predetermined 2002 construction and manufacturing employment shares as an exposure measure, I find that counties with greater concentrations of rate-sensitive industries experience systematically higher employment growth during monetary policy tightening. The contemporaneous interaction coefficient is 0.020 (p < 0.01), with the dominant effect materializing at a nine-month lag (β = 0.025, p < 0.01) and a cumulative four-quarter effect of 0.042 (p < 0.01). Results are robust across alternative base-year exposure measures and outcome specifications.

title: Life Satisfaction in Poland: The Role of Income, Unemployment and Age
affiliations: Warsaw School of Economics (SGH), Students and

detail.title: Life Satisfaction in Poland: The Role of Income, Unemployment and Age
detail.abstract: The article identifies the determinants of life satisfaction in Poland using representative CBOS surveys "Current Problems and Events" from 1999-2017. The analysis is embedded in the economics of happiness, with particular attention paid to income, labour market status and age as predictors of subjective well-being. The empirical part uses pooled cross-sectional CBOS data and estimates ordered logit models. The results show that higher household income per capita significantly increases the probability of reporting higher life satisfaction, while unemployment reduces it even after controlling for income. The relationship between age and life satisfaction is nonlinear, although the estimated minimum occurs later than in many international studies. The article contributes to research on well-being in Poland by using a long series of repeated representative surveys and by relating the findings to the economics of happiness and the literature on Poland's socioeconomic transformation.

title: Collective Commonality and Tactical Polyvalence: How the Public Sector Can Design Itself to Mitigate Industrial Disputes and Optimise Social Justice
affiliations: The Open University - Business School

detail.title: Collective Commonality and Tactical Polyvalence: How the Public Sector Can Design Itself to Mitigate Industrial Disputes and Optimise Social Justice
detail.abstract: While collective bargaining is a critical interdisciplinary topic, it is rarely analysed through the theoretical lenses of signalling theory (Spence, 1973), actor-network theory (Latour, 2005) or a combination of both theories. By utilising data from the British Social Attitudes Survey, the Labour Force Survey, and the OECD/AIAS ICTWSS database, this study adopts a multi-dataset quantitative approach. A two-way fixed effects regression reveals that trade union rights and annual wage growth rates have a significant effect on welfare expenditure decisions across OECD member states (Donado and Wälde, 2012); thus, the null of no correlation is rejected. Considering this direct fiscal impact, the thesis argues for the broader democratic necessity of collective bargaining, ultimately recommending the expansion of union rights in OECD countries facing restrictions on freedom of association.

title: On the Use of Failed Bids in Estimating the Treatment Effects of Mergers and Acquisitions

detail.title: On the Use of Failed Bids in Estimating the Treatment Effects of Mergers and Acquisitions
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the random assignment assumption underlying the quasi-experimental design that uses exogenously failed mergers. No merger failure is endogeneity-free, however, since withdrawal ultimately reflects a decision made by the firm. Moreover, potential heterogeneity in researchers' judgments when classifying failed bids undermines the reproducibility of research. Many deals classified as exogenously failed, such as those interrupted by competing bids, can alternatively be classified as endogenously failed, depending on the researcher's discretion. More importantly, I find evidence suggesting similarities between exogenously and endogenously failed acquirers. In tests of the market-timing theory of acquisitions, they exhibit similar stock performance, corroborating concerns about endogeneity in conventional exogenous failures. These findings indicate that empirical results in the literature depend critically on how and by whom firms are selected to serve as counterfactuals.

title: Profit Shifting and Firm Dynamics: Explaining the Selection into Tax Havens

detail.title: Profit Shifting and Firm Dynamics: Explaining the Selection into Tax Havens
detail.abstract: This paper provides a margin-based evaluation of international anti-profit-shifting policies. I develop a continuous-time heterogeneous-firm model in which firms choose whether to adopt a tax-haven structure and, conditional on adoption, how much profit to shift. The model separates three primitive margins: the organizational cost of haven adoption, the marginal cost of shifting, and the home-haven tax differential. Calibrated to 2019 U.S. data, it shows that adoption-margin reforms mainly change which firms use havens but leave aggregate shifted profits nearly unchanged, because marginal adopters are small and shift little. By contrast, enforcement that raises marginal shifting costs and rate coordination that compress tax differentials have larger direct effects on the tax base and welfare through public-good provision. In the calibrated Stackelberg game, a binding Pillar Two floor removes the haven's undercutting margin and raises welfare.

title: Developing a Simple and Intuitive Risk Metric for NPV Analysis

detail.title: Developing a Simple and Intuitive Risk Metric for NPV Analysis
detail.abstract: The net present value (NPV) is a fundamental tool in investment decision making within the field of corporate finance. NPV provides the financial manager with a binary outcome with one hundred percent certainty and no recognition of the likelihood of a negative NPV value. By bootstrapping market variations, we are able to create a distribution of possible NPVs for a project based on the relationship between the project's free cash flows, unlevered beta, and market returns. Unlike existing studies that apply bootstrapping or Monte Carlo simulations to NPV analysis, this proposed method does not require any discretionary decisions by the analyst. That is, the analyst is not required to choose which budget items to simulate or re-sample, nor does she have to assume the data generating process. This model is simple and generalizable to all NPV decisions. The probability of a negative NPV is an additional consideration that can be taken into account when making investment decisions. Applying modifications to the bootstrapping procedure in order to account for dependence in market variation is possible, as is demonstrated with a simple procedure to account for serial correlation and heteroskedasticity.

detail.abstract: Cities are uniquely positioned to combat noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and injuries. The investment case for cities to prioritize the prevention of NCDs and injuries should be self-evident, but for a variety of reasons is often low on decision-makers’ lists of priorities. Cities in low- and middle- income countries have additional challenges unique to their growing populations and the dynamics of economic development. But evidence from across the world, and new insights emerging from the Partnership for Healthy Cities show that interventions to combat NCDs and prevent injuries are critical, cost-effective, scalable, high-return investments in the present and future of healthy cities.

title: Risk, Return, and Anomalies in Islamic Equity Markets: A Post-2020 Review
affiliations: University of Malaya (UM)

detail.title: Risk, Return, and Anomalies in Islamic Equity Markets: A Post-2020 Review
detail.abstract:
Background: The rapid growth of the Islamic capital market has spurred significant
academic interest in developing and validating asset pricing models that adhere to Shariah
principles. Traditional models like the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) are often
inadequate due to their reliance on interest-based risk-free rates and assumptions that may not
hold in Shariah-compliant contexts.
Objective: This study conducts a systematic literature review of academic research published
between 2021 and 2025 to synthesize the current state of knowledge on asset pricing models
for Shariah-compliant stocks. It aims to identify the dominant models, key pricing factors,
and persistent anomalies, while highlighting methodological trends and research gaps.
Methods: Following the PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of Scopus and Web of
Science databases was conducted. The review focuses on studies examining the efficacy of
various pricing models, including the Shariah-Compliant Asset Pricing Model (SCAPM),
multi-factor models (e.g., Fama-French), and the Arbitrage Pricing Theory (APT), as well as
the influence of behavioral factors, ESG criteria, and downside risk.
Results: The review reveals a clear shift from traditional CAPM towards multi-factor
models, with the Fama-French five-factor model demonstrating superior explanatory power.
There is strong evidence of market segmentation, suggesting that Islamic-specific factors
better explain the cross-section of returns than market-wide factors. Key themes emerging
from recent literature include the outperformance of Islamic indices during crisis periods, the
significance of value and momentum premiums, and the growing influence of ESG and
behavioral factors in pricing Islamic equities.
Conclusion: The asset pricing landscape for Shariah-compliant stocks is evolving towards
more sophisticated, multi-factor frameworks that incorporate both financial and ethical
considerations. Future research should focus on developing more robust Islamic-specific
pricing factors, exploring the impact of new screening methodologies, and examining the
integration of Islamic markets with the global financial system.

title: Financial Literacy Education in Schools: Why Students Need Practical Money Management Skills

detail.title: Financial Literacy Education in Schools: Why Students Need Practical Money Management Skills

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved an anonymous student survey, interviews, and a focus group conducted for educational research purposes. No sensitive personal data was collected, and participants’ responses were used only in aggregated form.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Financial literacy is one of the most important life skills for young people, yet many students graduate from school without a clear understanding of budgeting, saving, spending, banking, or financial planning. This research investigates whether financial literacy should be taught in schools and how students currently manage their personal finances. The study used three research methods: an online survey, interviews, and a focus group. The survey collected responses from 101 students, while the qualitative part included three interviews and a focus group with five participants. The results show that most students receive pocket money and are interested in learning financial literacy, but many still manage their money superficially or spend it only when necessary without a clear plan. The study concludes that financial literacy education should be introduced as a practical, step-by-step subject starting from elementary school and continuing into high school. The proposed solution is a collection of sample financial literacy lessons based on real-life situations, budgeting exercises, simulations, and cooperation between schools and families.

title: The Comet Kernel and a Thorin Bridge to Xi
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Comet Kernel and a Thorin Bridge to Xi
detail.abstract: Kendall's stochastic model of long-period comets (1961), made analytic by Yabushita (1979), reduces a comet's history to a random walk in the energy variable absorbed at the origin (ejection) and killed at a rate set by a per-orbit fading probability. In the diffusion limit the survival kernel is an inverse Gaussian, equivalently the half-stable subordinator tempered at the fading rate. We give its Thorin measure in closed form and verify it through the cumulants; tempering translates the half-stable Thorin density rigidly to the right, so the fading parameter is the lower edge of the Thorin spectrum. We then expose the link to the Riemann XI-function: the very Laplace transform that defines the comet kernel is the half-stable subordinator that bridges Riemann's two Mellin representations of the completed zeta, carrying the heat/theta modes to the Cauchy modes. Under this bridge, fading maps to a spectral mass term, sending the massless lattice sum to the massive (Macdonald/Linnik) class. Summing the construction over the heat lattice gives a GGC whose Thorin measure is the Laplacian spectrum and whose Lévy density is the theta defect ψ/x; the same construction on the zeros makes RH the statement that the Xi Thorin measure is positive on reals (equivalently, Xi is Laguerre-Pólya). We keep a two-tier discipline throughout, marking the exact subordination identities off from the modular self-duality which the construction does not by itself supply.

title: Documentary Credits Under UCP 600: A Critical Comparative Analysis of Their Continuing Relevance in Modern Trade Practice

detail.title: Documentary Credits Under UCP 600: A Critical Comparative Analysis of Their Continuing Relevance in Modern Trade Practice
detail.abstract: Also known as letters of credit or LCs, Documentary credits form a cornerstone of international trade finance. They are primarily governed by the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (UCP 600) issued by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). Documentary credits are utilized to lessen risks such as non-delivery and nonpayment as they ensure trust between parties that are separated by legal, geographic, and cultural barriers. The following research critically adopts a structured approach and first introduces the strengths of documentary credits such as security and reliability. Then it outlines their deficiencies such as prohibitive costs and fraud vulnerabilities. Then a comparative analysis is made with concurrent payment methods such as blockchain solutions and open accounts. In the end, this article critically evaluates the benefits and challenges of documentary credits in a holistic manner and light of modern trade practices.

title: Do Remittances Increase Tax Revenue? The Conditional Role of Financial Inclusion in Africa
affiliations: University of Eldoret, Southwest University, Northwestern Polytechnical University and Universitas Lancang Kuning

detail.title: Do Remittances Increase Tax Revenue? The Conditional Role of Financial Inclusion in Africa
detail.abstract: Remittances represent a major source of external finance for developing economies, yet their contribution to domestic tax revenue remains theoretically ambiguous and empirically inconclusive. This study examines whether remittance inflows increase tax revenue in African countries and whether this relationship depends on the level of financial inclusion. Using panel data for ten major remittance-receiving African economies over the period 2004-2024, the paper employs a panel Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to estimate both short-run and long-run effects. To capture conditional dynamics, the analysis incorporates an interaction term between remittances and financial inclusion, allowing the effect of remittances on tax revenue to vary with the degree of financial system development. Additional controls include economic growth, trade openness, and corruption control. The results indicate that remittances have a positive and statistically significant impact on tax revenue in both the short and long run. Financial inclusion independently enhances tax revenue performance and plays a reinforcing role by strengthening the positive effect of remittances. The interaction term is positive and significant, suggesting that remittances contribute more effectively to tax revenue when financial systems facilitate the formalization of economic activity. This finding supports the view that the fiscal benefits of remittances operate primarily through consumption and formalization channels rather than through direct taxation. The study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that the remittance-tax revenue relationship is conditional rather than universal. It highlights the importance of financial inclusion as a structural mechanism that transforms external inflows into taxable economic activity. The findings imply that policies aimed at expanding financial access and promoting formal remittance channels can enhance domestic resource mobilization in African economies.

title: Growth, Accumulation & Deepening Dualism: Proliferation of a Fissured Informality /  A state and firm-level analysis in India
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Growth, Accumulation & Deepening Dualism: Proliferation of a Fissured Informality /  A state and firm-level analysis in India
detail.abstract: This paper examines the dynamics of India's informal sector in relation to the formal sector, critically interrogating growth-centric, inclusive, and convergent narratives of structural transformation in the Global South under contemporary capitalism. Focusing on both farm and non-farm informal sectors, the study analyses employment and income trends over the period 1999-2000 to 2022-2023. It employs a macro-structuralist framework to theorise the evolving structures of the informal sector in India and the formal sector's role within it. To empirically evaluate the theoretical propositions advanced in the paper, this study runs panel regression techniques (fixed-and random-effects models) and least squares dummy variable (LSDV) estimations based on state-and firm-level data of the non-formal sector, which includes both farm and non-farm informal sectors across two decades. The findings suggest that economic progress-manifested through formal sector expansion and/or infrastructural development has reproduced a fissured economic structure and deepened dualism within India's non-formal sector. While the traditional non-formal sector—dominated by own-account and petty production activities—continues to absorb a substantial share of the labour force, under conditions of declining income, segments of the modern non-formal sector have expanded alongside formal sector growth and show relatively stronger productivity performance.

title: Experimental Evidence for the HFT Arms Race: Welfare Decomposition and Market Fragility on a Formally Verified Limit Order Book

detail.title: Experimental Evidence for the HFT Arms Race: Welfare Decomposition and Market Fragility on a Formally Verified Limit Order Book

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The matching engine and simulation infrastructure were developed independently by the author.

detail.abstract: We provide an experimental test of the Budish-Cramton-Shim (BCS) theory of the highfrequency trading (HFT) arms race, conducted on a continuous limit order book whose matching core has been model-checked in TLA+ with zero invariant violations. Driving latency-differentiated snipers, an adverse-selection market maker, and noise traders through the verified engine via a pybind11 bridge, we decompose realized welfare into market-maker, noise-trader, and HFT components and find that HFT latency-arbitrage rent is a near-exact zero-sum transfer (residual at machine precision, mean) away from liquidity providers, accompanied by significantly more liquidity gaps. We then trace the mechanism across three further sweeps: rent scales approximately linearly in market-maker staleness with no detectable phase transition; as the number of HFTs grows, per-HFT rent dissipates as roughly while total extracted rent stays flat, so the marginal social cost of additional speed competition surfaces as rising fragility rather than rising rent; and frequent batch auctions recover market-maker welfare monotonically away from the degenerate single-tick interval (about 95% recovery by an interval of 500), with point estimates of rent also falling though more noisily. Because the matching layer is provably correct against its specification, the emergent arms-race dynamics cannot be attributed to engine artifacts, isolating them as consequences of rational latency competition on the continuous-clearing design itself.

title: Demand-Side Fee Flows and Return Predictability on Ethereum
affiliations: University of Regensburg and

detail.title: Demand-Side Fee Flows and Return Predictability on Ethereum
detail.abstract: We construct a protocol-native valuation signal for Ethereum based on demand-side fees expressed as a share of token supply. The signal measures the log deviation of current fee intensity from its trailing median, a dimensionless ratio denominated entirely in ETH. It predicts subsequent token returns at 10 to 60 day horizons with in-sample R-squared up to 22.8% and expanding-window out-of-sample R-squared of 14.4% at 45 days. The signal retains predictive power after macroeconomic controls, standard crypto risk factors, and momentum controls, and predicts ETH-specific relative returns. Predictability emerges only after the Dencun hard fork (March 2024), which separated execution fees from data availability fees, making the demand signal empirically detectable. Our findings demonstrate that demand-side economic flows are capitalized into token prices in the absence of firms, contracts, or residual cash flow rights, extending valuation logic to rule-based economic systems.

detail.abstract:
This report assesses how Gulf geopolitical tensions and potential Strait of Hormuz disruption affect Somalia’s trade-flow system, using Puntland, State of Somalia, as a case study. It situates Somalia within a highly import-dependent and externally exposed trade structure, where food, fuel, fertilizers, construction inputs, and other essential commodities are transmitted through fragile maritime corridors. The study applies a mixed-methods approach, combining secondary macroeconomic and trade data, port-level administrative information, CPI trends, and key informant interviews with market actors, including importers, fuel distributors, livestock exporters, LPG traders, and construction-material suppliers.

The findings show that Gulf-linked disruption does not simply create a temporary trade shock; it restructures Somalia’s commercial environment into a high-cost and low-predictability system. Rising freight charges, war-risk insurance premiums, fuel costs, and delivery delays have increased import costs and contributed to cost-push inflation. Puntland CPI evidence shows notable upward pressure from March 2026 in food, energy, cooking gas, and construction materials. On the export side, livestock trade remains highly vulnerable because it is seasonally concentrated around Hajj demand and heavily dependent on Gulf markets. Bosaso Port data indicates declining and volatile export vessel activity, while import flows remain high but irregular.

The report concludes that Somalia’s trade vulnerability is structural, reflecting import dependence, limited export diversification, climate stress, narrow fiscal capacity, and weak adaptive infrastructure. It recommends strategic food and fuel reserves, dedicated storage infrastructure, temporary controls on the re-export of strategic commodities, climate-resilient livestock systems, diversified export markets, and investment in domestic productive sectors.

title: Two-Rail Verification: A Public-Private Evidence-Separation Kernel for Institutional AI

detail.title: Two-Rail Verification: A Public-Private Evidence-Separation Kernel for Institutional AI

Related patent applications may be pending. No third-party certification, endorsement, patent license, or effective royalty-free pledge is claimed by this paper.
