title: Banking Stability as a Coordination Problem: Government Intervention, Confidence, and Moral Hazard.

detail.title: Banking Stability as a Coordination Problem: Government Intervention, Confidence, and Moral Hazard.
detail.abstract:
Abstract:
This paper models banking stability as a coordination problem rather than a balance-sheet problem. Using India’s monetary architecture as empirical motivation, where broad money (M3) stands at ₹313.6 trillion (approximately US$3.32 trillion) against physical currency in circulation (M0) of only ₹52.3 trillion (approximately US$552.97 billion), I show that simultaneous withdrawal by depositors would produce a liquidity crisis irrespective of bank solvency. The paper constructs a static coordination model in which depositors choose between withdrawing and continuing, and the government chooses whether to intervene. I demonstrate that government intervention stabilises depositor expectations but generates moral hazard, and that the credibility of any intervention commitment is undermined by a fiscal and logistical constraint, which this paper terms the M0 ceiling, the structural inability of physical currency distribution to keep pace with a confidence shock propagating through digital payment infrastructure processing over 600 million transactions daily. The paper concludes that neither unconditional guarantees nor conditional bailouts fully resolve the coordination failure, and that in a digitally enabled banking system, the central policy challenge shifts from whether the government can commit credibly to whether it can intervene fast enough to matter.

title: Speculative Supply Chains: How Rational Incentives Manufacture the Madness of Crowds

detail.title: Speculative Supply Chains: How Rational Incentives Manufacture the Madness of Crowds
detail.abstract:
A timeless question in financial markets is why extreme speculative episodes repeatedly emerge despite centuries of financial experience and increasingly sophisticated financial metrics. The two dominant philosophies of modern finance provide incomplete explanations. The Efficient Market Hypothesis implicitly assumes that rational behavior at the individual level aggregates into rational outcomes at the system level. Behavioral finance recognizes that investors often behave irrationally but offers limited insight into how irrationality scales into systemic speculative episodes.

This paper seeks to explain the phenomenon by introducing the concept of a speculative supply chain, which is defined as a network of financial intermediaries whose incentives become increasingly aligned toward the continuous deployment of capital. The framework proposes that speculative episodes arise not because market participants suddenly become irrational, but rather because rational decisions made by individuals and firms aggregate into collectively irrational outcomes. As speculative supply chains mature, incentives favoring capital deployment strengthen and become increasingly aligned across participant groups. Simultaneously, risk awareness becomes more segmented and corrective feedback is increasingly suppressed, which prevents most market participants from appreciating the growing gap between market narratives and long-standing economic principles.

Paradoxically, the framework suggests that speculative episodes become especially difficult to detect precisely when underlying conditions are becoming most dangerous. Warnings often remain publicly observable, yet their influence diminishes as incentives supporting continued capital deployment become more powerful than objective assessments of risk and return.

The implications for investors, regulators, and policymakers are significant. Rather than focusing exclusively on the vulnerabilities that produced the previous crisis, greater attention should be devoted to identifying the emergence, maturation, and migration of speculative supply chains that may be laying the foundation for the next one.

title: Control the Data, Not the Infrastructure A Mandatory Event-Reporting Architecture for Public Data Governance in Nepal

detail.title: Control the Data, Not the Infrastructure A Mandatory Event-Reporting Architecture for Public Data Governance in Nepal
detail.abstract: Nepal has built and procured digital identity, electronic procurement, payment, and agency information systems, but the state still lacks a dependable way to observe whether publicly funded systems are producing the public events promised by their contracts. This policytechnical working paper proposes a mandatory event-reporting architecture for public procurement and federal data governance in Nepal. The design is not a centralized megadatabase. It is a governance layer: every reportable public-sector event is submitted as a signed, hash-linked EventRecord to a National Data Registry, while source records remain with the agency or vendor system that created them. The lead use case is post-award procurement monitoring, especially IT systems that can be paid for without visible operational evidence. The second use case is citizen-service interoperability, where the National Identity Card and National Identity Number can act as lawful linking anchors without becoming a single citizen-profile database. The paper contributes a Nepal-specific schema, Reporting-Hook API contract, procurement rider, privacy and access-control model, threat model, costed pilot path, and phased implementation plan. It is framed as an architectural and legal blueprint for later software pilots, not as a claim of deployed empirical results.

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models

detail.title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
detail.abstract: This paper develops a geometric theory of identification for characteristic-based factor models under no-arbitrage restrictions. The central premise is that identification is governed not only by the statistical model but also by the metric that determines which directions in characteristic space are economically distinguishable. Existing approaches implicitly treat the Euclidean metric as the underlying ruler of characteristic space. We show instead that the long-run cross-sectional distribution of firm characteristics induces an empirical geometry that serves as a hidden ruler governing latent pricing directions. Within this geometry, latent and observable factors become structured subspaces, allowing identification, normalization, and no-arbitrage restrictions to be characterized as intrinsic geometric properties rather than algebraic constraints imposed on an estimator. Building on this framework, we derive a no-arbitrage formulation of Instrumented Principal Component Analysis that admits a projected weighted least-squares representation together with rotation-invariant asymptotic inference. The resulting information geometry separates latent, observable, and non-systematic components, establishing a unified statistical foundation for estimation and inference in high-dimensional characteristic spaces. Geometrycalibrated simulations demonstrate that identification depends fundamentally on the underlying metric: Euclidean representations become unstable in anisotropic characteristic spaces, whereas the proposed geometry consistently recovers economically meaningful pricing spans. The paper therefore develops a general geometric framework for identification and statistical inference under no-arbitrage, of which No-Arbitrage Instrumented Principal Component Analysis (NA-IPCA) constitutes one econometric realization.

title: Institutional Complementarities and Corruption Persistence: A Stochastic Dynamic Approach

detail.title: Institutional Complementarities and Corruption Persistence: A Stochastic Dynamic Approach
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unied theoretical framework for understanding the persistence of corruption in fragile institutional environments. We construct a two-stage model that combines microeconomic foundations with stochastic dynamic analysis. First, we establish three-player microfoundations Principal (State), Agent (civil servant), and Client (rm or citizen) within a game-theoretic and principal-agent framework, deriving six analytical propositions including the reservation bribe condition b * = µF/(1-µ), strategic complementarity between monitoring and wages, and the corruption trap as an institutional Nash equilibrium. Second, we embed these microfoundations in a six-dimensional stochastic dynamic system corruption C(t), institutional quality Q(t), extractive rents R(t), monitoring µ(t), real wages w(t), and social norms ρ(t) driven by Itô diusion with Poisson jumps. We prove existence and uniqueness of the strong solution, characterize the system's stochastic equilibria, and establish the Stochastic Big Push Proposition: escaping the corruption trap requires simultaneous modication of at least four institutional parameters. The model is motivated by the challenges of resource-rich, institutionally fragile economies the Democratic Republic of Congo serves as an illustrative reference point and a numerical exploration demonstrates the model's qualitative properties and generates testable hypotheses about the dynamics of corruption, the role of social norms, and the conditions for institutional transition.

detail.abstract: Generic drugs supply the large majority of prescriptions dispensed in the United States, yet a substantial share of their manufacturing now sits outside U.S. borders, and the timeliness of generic approvals remains a recurring concern. Much of the discussion of approval delay centers on the science of the abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) and on chemistry, manufacturing, and controls. This perspective isolates a different and under-leveraged contributor: facility readiness for pre-approval inspection. Drawing on U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance, the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments (GDUFA) III commitment letter, and federal oversight findings, it argues that an under-examined and preventable share of delay traces to facility-readiness and inspection-outcome problems that are knowable and addressable on the manufacturer side before an application is filed. The size of that share is not yet quantified; the contribution here is conceptual, and its measurement is identified as a direction for future work. The Form FDA 356h readiness certification offers a concrete illustration: a certification that a facility is not ready for inspection sets a 15-month goal date and defers substantive assessment until a readiness amendment is filed, so a preventable readiness gap converts directly into delay. The contribution is a manufacturer-side preventability framing of a problem usually treated as either scientific or as a matter of agency capacity.

detail.abstract:
Introduction. Multi-cycle assessment of abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) delays generic-medicine availability. GDUFA III (effective FY2023) introduced assessment enhancements intended to reduce the number of cycles. Whether this objective is yet observable in published performance data has not been examined.

Methods. From public FDA Generic Drugs Program Activities Reports, a fiscal-year series spanning GDUFA II (FY2018–FY2022) and GDUFA III (FY2023–FY2025) was assembled, the first public longitudinal GDUFA II-to-III comparison of first-cycle performance. The first-cycle approval rate proxied assessment-cycle efficiency, with complete-response volume, a workload-adjusted measure, and approval times as secondary measures.

Results. The first-cycle approval rate stayed within a narrow band (15.7%–19.9%; era means near 17.3% and 18.8%), within ordinary year-to-year variation, with no discontinuity at FY2023, and single-year endpoints partly denominator-driven. An illustrative power analysis indicates the observed 1.5-point difference would need roughly nine to twenty further years to detect, whereas a three-point shift would show within about two years, so three years cannot yet evaluate the goal. The workload-adjusted burden declined gradually, beginning before GDUFA III; approval times were non-monotonic; manufacturing and drug-product deficiencies predominated.

Discussion. The cycle-minimization objective is not yet detectable as a structural change, and the modest improvement present continues a trend already under way before GDUFA III.

Conclusion. The reported deficiency composition locates the predominant drivers in submission quality fixed at dossier preparation; whether this delay is preventable upstream remains a hypothesis for application-level testing. Durable cycle reduction may require dossier improvement alongside review-stage reform.

title: The Economic Impact of Inflation in Uzbekistan

detail.title: The Economic Impact of Inflation in Uzbekistan
detail.abstract: This study investigates the economic impact of inflation in Uzbekistan, with a particular focus on household consumption, purchasing power, and overall economic welfare. Using secondary data from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Central Bank of Uzbekistan, and Trading Economics, the research analyzes key macroeconomic indicators, including the Consumer Price Index (CPI), exchange rate movements, food price inflation, housing costs, and household consumption expenditure over the period 2011-2024. The findings indicate that although Uzbekistan has achieved partial success in reducing headline inflation, inflationary pressures remain persistent. Exchange rate depreciation, rising food prices, and increasing housing costs have significantly weakened household purchasing power and altered consumption patterns. Low-and middle-income households are disproportionately affected due to their greater reliance on essential goods. The study highlights the importance of continuous inflation monitoring and targeted policy interventions aimed at stabilizing prices, protecting household welfare, and supporting sustainable long-term economic growth in Uzbekistan.

title: How Digitalisation And Artificial Intelligence Can Create Competitive Advantages: Best Practice Applied To Strategic Business Management Within Professional Team Sports Companies

detail.title: How Digitalisation And Artificial Intelligence Can Create Competitive Advantages: Best Practice Applied To Strategic Business Management Within Professional Team Sports Companies
detail.abstract: This research explores how digitalisation can create competitive advantages in strategic management, both across industries and through its application in professional team sports. As data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) can be considered the central component of most digitalisation efforts, the study focuses on these two digital technologies. While digitalisation has become a priority across industries, a lack of definitional clarity still exists. Additionally, there remains a gap in the literature related to contextualising both the opportunities and limitations of digitalisation within a resource-based view and gaining competitive advantages by better decision-making. Furthermore, in relation to professional team sports, there is a gap in the academic literature regarding the role of data analytics and AI in decision-making within business functions (‘off-pitch’). Consequently, based on practical cross-industry examples, the research findings are applied to strategic ‘off-pitch’ business management. The research adopts a qualitative, abductive approach rooted in critical realism. The research purpose combines descriptive and exploratory types. Following a critical literature review, 20 in-depth expert interviews were conducted. Thematic analysis was applied to synthesise the findings, and eleven key themes were defined, with four having cross-industry relevance and seven focusing on sports analytics. By addressing four defined research questions, the study contributes theoretically by offering definitional clarity and linking strategic management theory with digitalisation. The study’s main practical contribution lies in providing a set of best practice examples to create a positive business impact, along with suggestions for overcoming potential limitations. Consequently, the work aims to serve as a ‘one-stop-shop’ for business leaders seeking to leverage data analytics and AI in professional team sports and beyond.

title: REMS-Restricted Drug Distribution Programs and the Antitrust Economics of Refusals to Deal with Potential Generic Competitors

detail.title: REMS-Restricted Drug Distribution Programs and the Antitrust Economics of Refusals to Deal with Potential Generic Competitors

keywords: Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act of 2007

detail.abstract:
The Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act of 2007 (FDAAA) grants the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) authority to require a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) from drug manufacturers to ensure that a certain drug's benefits outweigh its risks. Through REMS, the FDA restricts the distribution of drugs with dangerous characteristics, such as high toxicities and severe side effects, to qualified medical professionals. Such restrictions limit the ability of generic drug manufacturers to obtain samples of the REMS-restricted drugs for bioequivalence testing for an Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA). Without the ability to demonstrate bioequivalence in the ANDAs, potential generic entrants are unable to obtain FDA approval of drugs that would eventually compete with the REMS drugs. Recently, potential generic entrants have attempted to use the antitrust laws to force manufacturers of REMS-restricted drugs to provide them with samples. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has weighed in on behalf of generic entry.

The FTC’s recent actions are consistent with its long-standing policy concern regarding restrictions that limit generic drug competition. The FTC’s actions demonstrate its belief that generic entry in the pharmaceutical market will create positive consumer welfare effects. The consumer welfare effects of such generic competition, however, are more complex than merely lowered prices. Indeed, the FTC has downplayed evidence that generic entry restricts drug utilization, chills industry investment, and may have unintended health and safety consequences. Yet, the FTC has continued unabatedly down the path to generic drug nirvana, asserting that new entry by generics produces unambiguously positive effects for consumers.

The FTC’s recent intervention on behalf of generic manufacturers that attempt to use federal antitrust laws to gain access to REMS-restricted drugs overlaps with the FDA's direct oversight of REMS-restricted drugs. So long as original-brand manufacturing companies (brand manufacturers) have unanswered questions related to their liability for the actions of generic companies, they are unwilling to provide potential competitors with product samples, as there is no valid business justification to give up those samples. Rather, REMS-restricted drug makers have many valid business justifications for their refusal to deal with a potential generic manufacturer. This ongoing dispute has spurred private litigation and an FTC investigation. In two private litigation cases, the FTC filed amicus briefs claiming that the antitrust claims under section 2 of the Sherman Act are cognizable and that the court should determine the merits of the claim. To date, no court has addressed the merits of these antitrust claims and details of the FTC’s investigation are unclear. 

This Article provides an antitrust and economic analysis of a refusal-to-deal claim in the REMS context. The analysis suggests that the antitrust claims involved do not provide a proper justification for a new exception to a competitor's right to refuse to deal. The FDA and Congress play important roles in the complex regulatory scheme of the U.S. pharmaceutical industry. With so much regulation and oversight, antitrust has little place in ensuring an efficiently functioning market for REMS-restricted pharmaceuticals.

Part I provides background about generic drug entry under the Hatch-Waxman Act, which lays out the framework for ANDAs, and discusses REMS-restricted drugs under the FDAAA. This Part also details current antitrust litigation stemming from refusal to deal in the REMS context, as well as the FTC's position on such conduct. Part II summarizes the antitrust refusal-to-deal doctrine under section 2 of the Sherman Act by analyzing prior U.S. Supreme Court precedent. This Part then argues that refusal-to-deal claims in the REMS context fail under current refusal-to-deal jurisprudence. Part III argues that given the error costs associated with antitrust or agency intervention, such intervention would be contrary to public policy. Part IV suggests a narrow antitrust framework to analyze refusal to deal in the REMS context if the courts determine that antitrust analysis is appropriate. If the refusal to provide samples of REMS-restricted drugs to competitors does receive antitrust scrutiny, it should be evaluated under the profit-sacrifice test. Analysis under other theories of antitrust liability would be imprudent.

detail.title: Re-exploration of artisanal gold mining tailings in the Amazon increases mercury contamination
detail.abstract: The re-exploration of tailings from illegal artisanal gold (Au) mining is a highly prevalent activity in the Amazon due to residual Au content and low extraction efficiency. This activity increases risks to ecosystems and human health arising from mercury (Hg) enrichment in areas already contaminated by this element. Mercury enrichment and contamination, as well as environmental and human health risks, were assessed in artisanal Au mining tailings as a function of disposal time. Samples were collected and chemically characterized. For Hg concentrations, solubility and availability were also determined. Total Hg concentrations were elevated across all areas, particularly in the oldest site, which in turn exhibited lower values in the soluble and exchangeable fractions. Pollution indices indicated high levels of Hg contamination across all areas, with high to moderate environmental risk where soluble and available Hg concentrations were highest. Non-carcinogenic human health risks were detected in the tailings, particularly in the oldest material, via dermal exposure for adults and ingestion for children. Our findings indicate the need for mitigation and monitoring actions to minimize and prevent impacts on ecosystems and local population health, with potential extension to more remote areas such as indigenous lands and conservation units.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Sustainable Agricultural Supply Chains: Nash Equilibrium in Forward Contracts with Floor-Price Mechanisms for Smallholder Farmers

detail.title: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Sustainable Agricultural Supply Chains: Nash Equilibrium in Forward Contracts with Floor-Price Mechanisms for Smallholder Farmers
detail.abstract: This paper develops a three-player game-theoretic framework to address the inherent vulnerability and income instability of smallholder farmers in developing agricultural economies. By integrating a dynamic floor-price mechanism into forward contracts, we analyze the strategic interactions between farmers, middlemen (agribusinesses), and a regulatory buffer fund under a free-market paradigm. Unlike traditional contract models that heavily rely on severe punitive penalties to deter contract breaches-which often induce credit-rationing and participation aversion among low-income agents-our mechanism endogenizes the sharing of market surpluses during price spikes through a novel parameter: the Khanh coefficient (k). We mathematically prove the existence of a unique, self-enforcing Nash Equilibrium where cooperative supply chain behaviors are institutionalized. The model demonstrates that by dynamically adjusting the optimal Khanh coefficient (k*), the contract effectively mitigates the liquidity constraints of farming households during socioeconomic shocks while securing a stable supply of raw materials for buyers, minimizing the necessity of direct state intervention.

title: The Single-Use Architecture of Philanthropic Capital: Why the Grant's Defining Feature Is Also Its Defining Constraint

detail.title: The Single-Use Architecture of Philanthropic Capital: Why the Grant's Defining Feature Is Also Its Defining Constraint

detail.abstract: The grant is the default instrument of philanthropy, so familiar that it is rarely examined as a capital structure at all. This paper argues that the grant's defining feature-that it is given once and not returned-is not merely a generous design choice but a structural commitment with systematic consequences, and that those consequences explain a substantial share of philanthropy's persistent underperformance against its own goals. A grant is single-use capital: it funds an activity once and is then consumed, regardless of whether that activity created recoverable value, durable capability, or returnable surplus. This architecture produces three endemic failures. Value leakage : surplus, capability, and intellectual property generated by grant-funded work escape the philanthropic system rather than recycling within it, with the largest leakage occurring in the most successful grants. Dependency by design : because the instrument contains no mechanism to convert a recipient's success into independence, it structurally rewards renewal over self-sufficiency, irrespective of recipient quality or funder intent. The deployment-once horizon : a granted dollar works only once, so total social production from a corpus is capped by its size rather than its velocity, whereas any positive recovery rate multiplies lifetime output from the same pool. The paper shows that these are properties of the single-use form itself, not of poor grantmaking, and that the field's reform vocabulary-multi-year, unrestricted, and trust-based fundingimproves the experience of the instrument without altering its architecture. It closes by distinguishing the cases where single-use is genuinely optimal-emergency relief, pure public goods, and dignity transfers, all marked by the absence of recoverable value-from the much larger set where a recoverable, recycling instrument would produce more social value from the same corpus, forward-citing the recoverable-grant instrument, its contractual architecture, and Regenerative Capital Theory.

title: The Perpetuity Trap: Why Foundation Endowments Misallocate Capital

detail.title: The Perpetuity Trap: Why Foundation Endowments Misallocate Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The perpetual foundation-an endowment designed to exist indefinitely while distributing only a small fraction of its corpus each year-is treated as the default architecture of institutional philanthropy, a neutral container for serious charitable intent. This paper argues that perpetuity is not a neutral container but a capital structure with its own logic, and that this logic is systematically misaligned with the missions it is meant to serve. The misalignment is structural rather than behavioural: a foundation operating a perpetual endowment is bound by two fiduciary duties-a duty to preserve the corpus and a duty to advance the mission-and the real-terms preservation mandate forces the first to dominate the second, so that the institution is optimised for its own survival rather than the resolution of the problem. The paper traces three failure modes that follow from this conflict and reproduce regardless of the quality or sincerity of trustees: corpus primacy , in which the institution's perpetuity structurally outranks the problem's urgency and the mission becomes the residual; the payout floor as ceiling , in which the regulatory minimum distribution-a figure reverse-engineered from preservation rather than need-becomes the operative maximum; and horizon inversion , in which capital is held longest precisely where the social return to early deployment is highest. It shows that the conventional reforms-higher payout rates, mission-related and program-related investment, and spend-down commitments-are within-structure adjustments that soften symptoms while leaving corpus primacy intact, and that this is why the perpetuity trap is a trap rather than a flaw: the structure constrains the very remedies its stewards can adopt. The paper closes by specifying the conditions a capital architecture aligned to mission cycles rather than institutional survival would have to satisfy-capital that recycles rather than depletes, return horizons synchronised to mission horizons, and measurement across cycles-and by reframing the fiduciary question itself: from the stewardship of a corpus over the life of an institution to the stewardship of a problem over the life of its resolution.

detail.abstract: Digital customer service has become an important component of telecommunications transformation. However, the availability of digital channels does not automatically lead to frequent or sustained customer adoption. This paper develops an unpublished MSc Business and Management research project completed in 2019 into an applied research paper on digital customer service adoption barriers, focusing on a major telecommunications operator in the Arab Gulf, which remains anonymized for confidentiality reasons. The study used a quantitative survey design and collected 271 valid customer responses. The findings showed that digital channel adoption was still developing: 41.0% of respondents used digital channels frequently, 43.5% used them sometimes, and 15.5% had never used them. The main barriers were linked to limited awareness of digital channel benefits, incomplete availability of required functions, slow request completion, complexity of use, preference for human interaction, trust concerns, and cases where digital interactions did not fully resolve customer needs. The paper positions the 2019 study as an empirical baseline for understanding digital customer service adoption barriers during an important period of telecommunications digitalization in the Arab Gulf. It argues that improving digital adoption requires more than expanding the number of digital channels. Effective adoption depends on awareness, functional completeness, speed, trust, usability, service quality, and successful service completion. The findings are discussed at a sector level, with contextual relevance to the digital transformation direction that emerged in Saudi Arabia and the wider region following the launch of Vision 2030.

title: Why Blended Finance Underperforms: A Structural Diagnosis of the Catalytic Claim

detail.title: Why Blended Finance Underperforms: A Structural Diagnosis of the Catalytic Claim

detail.abstract: Blended finance is endorsed across development and impact capital as the mechanism that mobilises private investment toward public goods, using concessional capital to de-risk commercial returns. Yet after a decade of institutional uptake, mobilisation has stagnated and its central catalytic claim remains largely unverified. This paper argues that the underperformance is structural rather than operational: blended finance assembles its instruments from single-cycle, liability-bearing components-tranches, guarantees, first-loss layers-and applies them to objectives that are inherently multi-cycle and relational, realised across a sequence of transactions rather than at the resolution of any one. From this single mismatch the paper derives three failure modes. Horizon collapse consumes concessional capital within the cycle rather than recycling it across cycles. The de-risking paradox biases the instrument toward subsidy that resembles catalysis at deployment, with no structural means to distinguish the two. And measurement at the deployment boundary renders the catalytic claim unfalsifiable in the field's own terms, because catalysis is defined across a cycle boundary the instrument does not represent. Each failure is shown to be endemic to the instrument design rather than incidental to its execution, and each would persist under flawless operation. The paper closes by specifying three conditions-derived directly as inversions of the failure modes-that any non-extractive, multi-cycle alternative would need to satisfy, and by drawing out the implications for catalytic-capital allocators, for whom the decisive choice is shown to precede transaction selection entirely.

title: The End of English as the Sole Language of Global Coordination

detail.title: The End of English as the Sole Language of Global Coordination
detail.abstract: English is the native tongue of roughly five to seven percent of humanity, yet it operates as a mandatory entry requirement across the systems that govern modern life: international aviation, scientific publishing, global finance, diplomacy, and higher education. This paper does not argue that English should be removed from these systems. It argues something narrower and more defensible: that a contingent historical outcome, the spread of one language through empire and postwar economic dominance, has hardened into a structural requirement whose costs are now measurable, whose justification was always coordination rather than merit, and whose technical premise has changed. The paper offers a three-axis test, temporality, severity and irreversibility of error, and breadth of content, and applies it not as a binary but as a spectrum, accepting the test's verdict even in cases such as maritime distress where it rules for a shared language. Drawing on quantitative evidence of the disadvantages borne by non-native English speakers in science, on the language-coverage data of the major citation databases, on the safety rationale embedded in international aviation law, and on the deliberately language-neutral architecture of the ISO 20022 financial-messaging standard, it argues that machine translation has begun to dissolve the coordination rationale unevenly, fully for highresource asynchronous tasks, not yet for low-resource languages or the safetycritical core, so that the live injustice is institutions mandating English where the justification has already lapsed. The argument is framed against the oldest question in political philosophy, whether might makes right, and answered in the negative: dominance explains English's position but does not justify its permanence. The paper closes with proposals that distinguish mandated dominance from emergent equilibrium and parity-by-technology from parity-by-investment, arguing for parity rather than replacement.

title: Extraneous Influences in Collective Decision-Making: Evidence from Atmospheric Conditions
affiliations: Massey University and

detail.title: Extraneous Influences in Collective Decision-Making: Evidence from Atmospheric Conditions
detail.abstract: We examine how extraneous, non-substantive factors influence complex collective decision-making in settings where empirical identification is challenging and outcomes carry allocative and welfare implications. Primarily drawing on over 20,000 legislative votes across North America, we document a positive relation between sky clarity and the proportion of yea votes, with increasingly pronounced effects as vote margins narrow. This relation persists after controlling for location-by-week fixed effects and unpleasant weather conditions, attenuates with repeated exposure (consistent with habituation), and disappears under simulations of seasonal sky conditions with stochastic perturbations. Counterfactual analyses suggest that alternative sky conditions could have altered outcomes in close votes, highlighting the potential for extraneous factors to shape policy choices. Overall, the findings underscore the general importance of grounding decisions in fundamentals, as even subtle extraneous influences can materially distort outcomes beyond legislative decisions.

title: Cohort-Based Regression Discontinuity Designs with Fixed-Quota Cutoffs

detail.title: Cohort-Based Regression Discontinuity Designs with Fixed-Quota Cutoffs

detail.abstract:
This paper studies regression discontinuity designs in which treatment is assigned by a fixed quota within cohorts. Unlike canonical RD designs, where treatment changes at an externally fixed cutoff of a running variable, many policies allocate treatment to the top fraction or top number of units within a cohort. Examples include scholarships awarded to the top students in a class, honors programs admitting the top applicants from each school, and percent-plan admission policies based on high-school class rank. In such settings, the cutoff is not a fixed score. It is a cohort-specific sample quantile.

This paper develops a framework for interpreting RD designs with fixed-quota cutoffs. In large cohorts, sample-quantile cutoffs are first-order equivalent to population quantile cutoffs under standard local-polynomial bandwidth conditions. In many small cohorts, however, the empirical cutoff does not converge to a population threshold. The natural object becomes a finite-cohort rank-margin assignment contrast rather than a population score-cutoff causal effect. This contrast has a causal interpretation only under additional assumptions that make adjacent marginal ranks locally comparable. The paper also shows that percentile-rank transformations create an information-loss problem: ranks preserve order but discard score spacing, so diagnostics based only on ranks do not directly test continuity of the underlying score density. The paper clarifies when cohort-based quota RD behaves like ordinary score-based RD, when it becomes a rank-based design, and how empirical researchers should interpret estimands and diagnostics under fixed-quota assignment rules.

detail.title: Energy Prices, Emissions, and Workforce Composition in Norwegian Manufacturing
detail.abstract: This paper examines how carbon policy, proxied by energy price shocks, affects firms’ labor demand, environmental performance, and workforce composition in a highly electrified economy. Using panel data for Norwegian establishments from 2009–2022 and a shift-share instrument based on energy input mixes and national price fluctuations, we estimate the effects on employment, wages, emissions, and skill composition. We find that higher energy prices substantially reduce energy use and CO2 emissions, while having limited effects on aggregate employment and wages. Evidence of within-establishment reallocation is modest: occupational changes are small, but educational composition shifts slightly toward more highly educated workers, consistent with mild workforce upgrading. Overall, the results suggest that carbon pricing can deliver environmental gains with limited labor-market disruption, while also inducing a gradual rebalancing toward higher-skilled labor.

detail.abstract:

Because inbound restrictions on foreign tokens and issuers are systematically tighter than outbound treatment, and because the inbound mechanism differs jurisdiction by jurisdiction, corridors are modeled as one hun dred thirty-two directed edges rather than sixty-six undirected pairs. Each edge is assigned a composite feasibility class, a governing inbound mechanism with its named administrator, an infrastructure overlap, a set of carried corridor archetypes, the operative interaction sets from the Architecture working paper, and, where the origin imposes an export or egress restriction, an origin-override flag. Ten recurring corridor dimensions, from sanctions and lawful-order capability to holder-identification depth, are promoted to a first-class dimension reference. 

The Atlas serves two audiences. For an operator, it is a routing reference that states, for a given direction of flow, what authorization or recognition is required and which mechanism gates the corridor. For a supervisor or researcher, it is a stakeholder database that maps each category of participant to the corridor dimension that most directly determines its options. All claims rest on the public regulatory record as of late June 2026 and defer to the Compliance Matrix for the version-stamped jurisdictional facts; forward-looking items are flagged with conditional status.

title: Inflation as an Emergent Phenomenon
affiliations: and Polytechnic University of Marche - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Inflation as an Emergent Phenomenon
detail.abstract: We develop an agent-based model in which inflation emerges from decentralized price-setting and credit-financed production in an endogenous-money economy. Firms operate under working-capital constraints, form market-based price expectations through heterogeneous adaptive learning, and set prices via cost-plus rules with endogenous markups. Bank lending simultaneously creates deposits, while heterogeneous lending rates and credit rationing shape firms' financing costs and, through unit costs, their pricing decisions. The economy features interacting production and credit networks: intermediate-input linkages propagate cost shocks across supply chains, while bank-firm relationships transmit financial conditions across firms. The interaction of network-based pass-through, state-dependent pricing incentives, and evolving credit conditions generates inflationary regimes, including episodes driven by pricing cascades and feedback loops.

title: Supplier Enforcement and the Opioid Crisis
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: Supplier Enforcement and the Opioid Crisis
detail.abstract: Federal enforcement of the Controlled Substances Act, which obligates prescribers, pharmacies, and distributors to prevent opioid diversion, is a central policy lever for addressing opioid-related harms, yet its effectiveness remains poorly understood. This paper studies these interventions using novel data on DEA enforcement actions linked to firm-level data on opioid shipments. It is the first analysis of enforcement across all three levels of the opioid supply chain, and the first to identify its effects from within-state variation in both the timing and intensity of enforcement. Enforcement against prescribers reduced opioid supply nationwide; enforcement against pharmacies and distributors reduced it only where diversion and enforcement activity were most concentrated over this period, in Florida. I provide direct evidence on mechanisms underlying these heterogeneous responses: isolated actions tend to be offset as rival suppliers expand, while concentrated enforcement in an area deters even those not directly prosecuted. I further show that distributor enforcement was well-targeted, reaching distributors with weak diversion controls whose highest-risk customers were least able to substitute. In Florida, enforcement actions collectively averted roughly 2,400 opioid overdose deaths, implying averted mortality costs about ten times what the DEA spent on its diversion control program. Overall, these findings highlight that supply-side enforcement is not uniformly effective, but can substantially reduce mortality when focused on disrupting concentrated sources of diversion activity.
